Sir LOMER GOUIN (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 93 to amend the Criminal Code.
He said: This bill is a short one, and the principal clauses in it contain amendments raising the ages of girls, in the case of indecent assault, from 14 to 16, and carnally knowing from 14 to 16; removing the words "of previous chaste character" in the latter case; and repealing an amendment inserted in the Senate in 1920 that in the case of seduction and for carnally knowing a girl between 14 and 16 the trial judge may instruct the jury that, if in their view the evidence does not show that the accused is wholly or chiefly to blame for the commission of the offence, they may find a verdict of acquittal. These provisions were all passed by the House of Commons last year but were rejected in the Senate. In addition to these there is a provision extending the provisions about bribing police officers to police commissioners; and one correcting a technical error with respect to section 244. This section imposes a penalty for the offences mentioned in the three preceding sections, but by an amendment some sections were added to the code and inserted in the middle of these three sections so as to raise a doubt as to the application of section 244. There is a provision to protect English hall marks on gold and silver; a provision to remove a doubt as to what the maximum penalty should be for stealing an automobile; an amendment to the section with respect to the carriage of animals by railways, to do away with the necessity of getting a written request from the owner to enable the railway to keep the animals the maximum time in the cars, that is, 36 hours; a repeal of the section giving the clerk and deputy clerk of the peace at Montreal and Three Rivers certain powers of justices-the repeal of this section has been requested by the Attorney General's Department of Quebec-a provision giving municipalities of Ontario the j fines when they bear the expense of administering the law under which the same are imposed instead of paying them to the province as at present; and an amendment extending the provisions of section 1038, which enables certain penalties to be recovered by civil process, so as to make it include corporations.

Reference was made yesterday by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) to a question which was put to the Government some days ago in regard to a certain judgment which was rendered by the Court of Appeal of Manitoba in connection with the Canada Grain Act. As soon as I came into possession of the judgment and the notes of the judges I studied the case. I had a conference with my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) and the member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales), to whom I intimated my views of the case. They both requested an opportunity of meeting the members of the board before anything should be decided upon. I acceded to the request and was governed accordingly. The members of the board, I may say, arrived in Ottawa this morning, or last night. This morning they had a conference with the Minister of Trade and Commerce at which I understand, the member for Saltcoats was also present. They informed me a few minutes before the opening of the House to-day that they had not yet arrived at any final decision but would come to a conclusion during the course of the day. To-morrow, therefore, I hope to be in a position to make a statement to the House as to what decision the Government will take in the matter.
Supply Bill
On the Orders of the Day:

I desire to call the attention of
the House and of the Government to a matter of great concern to the province of Manitoba. I refer to the overflowing of the river Assiniboine. As hon. members have no doubt read in the papers, a great deal of land has been flooded in the constituency of Brandon, and the destruction has spread further east until now Portage la Prairie, which I have the honour to represent, is affected. I have no definite information as to the total destruction caused by the flood, but it will be seen from the press reports that considerable damage has already been done. Carcasses of horses, cattle and pigs, and the wreckage of granaries and outbuildings are to be seen floating down the river. Last night I sent a telegram to the editor of The Free Press at Winnipeg with a view to securing some information that I might submit to Parliament, but unfortunately I have not yet received an answer. However, as I have said, considerable damage has been done already, and perhaps there will be further destruction still. I would not bring this matter to the attention of the House if I did not think it my duty to do so. I believe that the federal government in the past has spent sums of money in building dykes along this river to keep back the flooding waters in the spring. I do not know how much they have spent for the purpose, but the fact is that they have expended money on this work, and I believe they assumed responsibility for the waters flooding the country. I have nothing to suggest, but I think it would be all right if the Government would
Order. I would ask the hon. member to kindly put his question to the Government as tersely as possible. There can be no argument on the Orders of the Day.
The question I would ask the Government is this: Do they intend to do anything to alleviate the sufferings of those people along the Assiniboine river?

Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of the Naval Service): Mr. Chairman, I want to make a short statement to the committee; it may help to guide its deliberations. Hon. gentlemen opposite will not, I am sure, attribute to me any considerable degree of modesty. In the course of the remarks I made the other day on the appropriation for the Royal Canadian Navy, I used these words:
I suggested to the officers that we could divide these ships, send one or two of them to the Pacific coast and keep one of them on the Atlantic coast. I had an idea that the Aurora could be used on the Atlantic, and this shows my absolute unacquaintance with the naval service and what a navy is supposed to do.
A little further down I said:
This, the officer told me, was absolutely out of the question; if we separated those ships and sent two of the destroyers to the Pacific coast, those destroyers would not do at all for the purposes of training by themselves and would be wholly unsuitable for the pelagic sealing protection.
Now, the Director of the Naval Service tells me that I was too modest about myself and too emphatic about him. I will not admit either, but I want to state the attitude which the Director of the Naval Service says he took. He strongly favoured the retaining of the squadron, and he insists that he did not assure me that he could not use any unit of this squadron to assist in carrying out the scheme that I had in mind. I understood his attitude as I stated it, but life is too short to quarrel about it, so I accept his word that I misunderstood him. Some day I may get him to accept mine that he misunderstood me, but not to-day. Now, I am pleased to announce to the committee that the Director of the Naval Service assures me that the first suggestion I made, or a portion of it, is practicable, namely, that one of the torpedo boat destroyers can be used on the Pacific and one on the Atlantic; that the volunteers for the naval service can be trained on these two destroyers, in gunnery, seamanship, and all lines pertaining to the naval service, so far as that training is carried out on a ship of that size. The corrected suggestion I have to make is this: I propose to ask the committee to sanction the use of these two torpedo boat
Supply-Naval Service

destroyers as suggested, instead of the two small ships mentioned in the outline of a few days ago.
I want to correct a little misconception which, I think, exists with regard to these trawlers. My idea of a trawler -and this, I suppose, would be the idea of most hon. gentlemen-would be that it is something in the way of a small fishing smack. These trawlers, however, are seagoing craft, 130 feet long, each carrying a 12-pound gun and manned by from twenty to thirty men. Some thirty or thirty-five of these trawlers were in commission on the coasts of Canada during the war, and rendered wonderful service. I am informed that our share of the patrol of the Pribyloff islands, involving work which we agreed to perform but which for several years we have not done, can be carried out by a craft of the nature I have described. The revenue cutters of the United States are not large ships. They are larger than these, but the Director of the Naval Service assures me that there would be no difficulty in having one of these so-called trawlers proceed to the seal fishing area and patrol those waters. In order that hon. gentlemen may understand that part of the undertaking with respect to the seal fisheries of the Pribyloff islands which we have not performed, I will read a memorandum which has been prepared on the subject:
On July 7th, 1911, a treaty was signed at Washington between Great Britain, United States of America, Japan and Russia for the adoption of means looking to the preservation and protection of the fur seal in the Bering Sea. Under the terms of this treaty the nations interested agreed to prohibit their nationals from engaging in pelagic sealing in the waters of the Pacific Ocean north of the 30° of north latitude. The nations interested undertook to carry on such patrol as would be necessary to enforce the terms of the treaty.
In August, 1910, the Colonial Office had asked if Canada could take part in the Bering Sea patrol and on October 22nd, of the same year, an Order in Council was passed stating that the revenue vessels of the Canadian Government on the Pacific coast were too small for this service, but that the vessels which it was proposed to obtain for the Canadian Naval Service could undertake the patrol and that as soon as the ships were built and equipped Canada would be prepared to send one or more of them to do patrolling within the limits specified.
On September 21st, 1911, the Colonial Office wrote to the Canadian Government stating that the British Admiralty were "prepared to arrange that a vessel of the Imperial Navy should carry out the patrol in the waters North of 30° north latitude and east of the meridian of 170° west longitude until vessels of His Majesty's Canadian Navy were available for carrying out this service."
I Mr. Graham. ]
The limits suggested were those of the Canadian Pacific (Station. The patrol was to be a joint one with the United States. Patrol of the Pacific Ocean west of the 170th meridian was to be carried out by Russia and Japan jointly.
After this date the British Admiralty maintained two sloops, the "Shearwater" and the "Algerene" on the Pacific station for the purpose of this patrol.
In May, 1914, the Colonial Secretary asked if the Canadian Government could detail H.M. C.S. "Rainbow" to undertake this patrol. The "Rainbow" had been out of commission for some time but she was prepared for sea, placed in commission and was sailing for Behring Sea when news was received that war was imminent. She was therefore detained and on the declaration of war took up her duties as a cruiser in the P'acific Ocean, and no British ship has attended to the Behring Sea patrol since that date, the patrol being effected by United States vessels.
Canada is very interested in the question of pelagic sealing and derives a considerable income from the killing of the seals on the Pribylof Islands. She should therefore take part in the patrol and have a vessel available for inspection of the Pribylof Islands and the killing grounds so as to ascertain for herself how the treaty is being carried out and what results are being obtained.
The revenue obtained in 1919 for Canada's share of the sales of skins from the Pribilof Islands was $266,000. Prices of skins have gone down and last year the amount realized was $65,000. In April of this year a sale was held which netted Canada $23,000. Another sale will be held in the fall.
It will be observed, therefore, that Canada agreed to carry on this patrol, or, at least, to insipect the work and see that it was properly carried out and that treaty obligations were respected; and also that we have a financial interest in seeing that this is done. The Director of the Naval Service assures me that this work can be performed and Canada put in a better position than she has been since the signing of this treaty in regard to her share of the patrol of the sea fishing areas in Behring sea.

I understand that
under the Pelagic Sealing Treaty, which was negotiated in Washington, nationals of all parties to the treaty, such as Russia, Japan, United States and Canada, were to be prohibited from engaging in the seal fisheries. It was understood, however, that at certain seasons of the year a certain number of seals were to be caught and sold and the proceeds divided among the various parties to the agreement. How does the revenue derived by Canada from the sale of these seals compare with the cost of the patrol?

speechtext: Yes; at any rate it provided that Canada should look after any patrol which the British admiralty engaged to carry out under that agreement. But, so far as I can ascertain, Canada has not undertaken that work, although she has been getting receipts from the seal fisheries.

speechtext: We can get the figures from the Department of Fisheries. I am told that from one sale that was held our share was $23,000, and that there is to be another sale this fall.
Has the Pelagic Sealing Treaty been denounced, or are we still working under it?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The treaty is still in existence, and the United States is doing her share of the patrol work, and so, I believe are Russia and Japan.
As to the submarines, as I announced a few days ago, the Government's policy is not to retain the submarines in commission. The use of the submarine in warfare is a question about which there has been a great deal of discussion among the great nations of the world during the past few months. It was discussed at some length at Washington; it has been discussed elsewhere, and I presume that it will be discussed in the future at other places, perhaps at the Genoa Conference. I think it is well to point out to the committee now that this action of the Government has a pretty strong foundation. I admit at once that there are those who argue, and argue strongly, that the submarine for defence purposes is very useful, one reason that is advanced for its usefulness being that only a submarine with its hydrophone system can detect the approach of similar vessels, that vessels that do not submerge cannot perform this service. Nevertheless, it will be remembered that strong ground was taken at the Washington Conference by several representatives of the great nations, of Great Britain, in particular, as to whether the submarine should be retained at all. There were some, if I remember the reports of the conference aright, who favoured the total abolition of the submarine in future warfare. Others took the opposite view. I am pointing this out to the committee to show that, to use ordinary language, in tying up the submarines, the Government of Canada is following a very dependable lead.
In tabling a return to an Order of the House on the 11th of April last, containing the documents of the Cannes Conference,' the Prime Minister said, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Mar. quette (Mr. Crerar)-I quote from unrevised Hansard, page 902:
I therefore beg to present:
1.	Copy of Memorandum on Anglo-French relations and of the draft of the proposed treaty with France presented by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom to Mr. Briand at the meeting of the Supreme Council at Cannes, January. 1922.
2.	Copy of Resolutions adopted by the Supreme Council at Cannes, January, 1922, as the basis of the Genoa Conference.
I find in the memorandum presented officially by the British government these words:
The third is the question of submarines. His Majesty's Government make no condition of this, and they fully understand that the divergencies of French and British views on the subject may be due to different ideas of the uses which submarines can serve. The British opinion, however, based on four years' war experience, is that submarines are effective only against merchant ships and are ineffectual otherwise as instruments either of attack or defence.
I think that is about as strong language as could possibly be used in reference to the use of the submarine. So I submit for the information of the House, as it may help in the discussion of this item, that in putting the submarines out of commission the Canadian government is following the exact lead of the British Admiralty and its policy is in harmony with the official declarations of the British government's representatives gathered together in conference with the great nations of the world.

Now that France and the other assembled nations at the Washington Conference have declined the British lead of abandoning the submarine, is it a fact that Great Britain herself has abandoned the submarine?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would not say that Great Britain has, but that does not affect the argument that the submarine has been declared by Great Britain not to be a success, either in attack or defence, except against merchant vessels. This is a question that I suppose will be discussed more or less at conferences in the future.
I want to point out to the committee that this proposal, as announced the other day in the House, is not a finality on naval policy. There is no finality on naval policy
Supply-Naval Service

in the whole world to-day. The great nations of the world will probably meet several times again before they arrive at a conclusion as to the restriction or development of armaments, including the navy, and conferences will be held by the Overseas Dominions as to what share they ought to take. According to the report, such a conference was provided for at the conference held recently. The policy of the Government is along the lines and in accordance with the Naval Service Act passed in 1910. There is not a suggestion in it that is not contained within the paragraphs of the act of 1910. While all countries of the world are wondering at the present time what policy they will finally adopt for attack and defence, Canada is proceeding along safe, sane, economical lines, and when the time comes that a future policy is to be decided upon, we shall have a foundation on which can be built a naval policy worthy of Canada, if the Parliament of Canada decide on development.
I do not know that I need say anything more. I wanted to make this explanation about the submarines, the trawlers, and the torpedo boat destroyers, so that the committee would not be discussing the matter without knowing the full facts.

The minister stated a moment ago that there was no finality about this proposal. Well, it is pretty near to finality. We would not have much further to go to make it final. I think the minister this afternoon has been in somewhat deep water.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Where else should the navy be?

He has been labouring pretty hard. His statement this afternoon is not at all in accordance with the statement of policy which he made on Friday afternoon. He has undergone another change of heart, and a most radical one, and has laboured in pretty deep water this afternoon in an effort to explain it. It was not surprising to those of us who sit in this corner of the House. It was remarked on the streets of Toronto yesterday that we would have another flop here in naval matters; and I have no doubt in my mind that when the minister and the government read the Toronto Globe's editorial on Saturday, the process of changing heart and changing policies at once began, and we have the result of that Change to-day. Now it is amusing for all members to sit and listen to my hon. friend's explanation this afternoon of the reason why he was

going to abandon these two submarines. That is not the reason he gave on Friday. Why, on Friday the announcement he made to the House was that he was going to abandon the naval service and to go into the volunteer service. That was his reason for stating the policy which he then gave, but in the interval he has had to take up some communications that passed between the French government and British government on the programme that was laid down and discussed at Cannes; and he came to the House this afternoon with a radical change of policy simply because he found from his own friends and his own prominent supporters outside of this House, that the scrapping process which he announced on Friday afternoon was not going to meet with the approval of the rank and file of his party throughout the Dominion. I do not think it was very hard for my hon. friend to take a somersault, or for the members of the Government to take a somersault; they must be quite used to that sort of thing during the present session. It is a spectacle which has ceased even to amuse hon. members in this corner of the House under the conditions which have existed since the session opened.
Now what my hon. friend proposes is simply this: To take the five ships which were a gift by Great Britain to this country and which were accepted by it in good faith-
No, no.
To take those five ships and scrap them, save two which he says now he finds he can use as training ships.
Ships that were asked for.

the approval of this House and the approval of the Admiralty, will only cost two and a half millions. The greater scheme is in itself a most modest one and is not expensive, but it may yield some results and may train some men. It may eventually amount to something and be of some real value to the country. But it looks to me as if it were going to be pure waste of money to spend a million and a half a year on a volunteer service such as described by my hon. friend on Friday last.
I am not alone in that opinion. I read it in the Toronto newspapers, and I see it in the editorials in the Montreal newspapers. You might just as well throw your money in the ocean as to spend a million and a half on any such scheme as was outlined by the hon. minister on Friday afternoon. I think he has tried to improve his scheme between last Friday and to-day, because he knows it is absolutely unworkable. Well, what are we going to do? Are we going to spend a million and a half of money in playing at naval warfare, getting together a few naval volunteers in this country, and bringing them down to the sea for two weeks each year as a sort of holiday? It is not going to get us anywhere, or establish anything in the nature of a permanent naval service. I believe there is only too much in the criticism that it will be an absolute waste of money. Why can the minister not be content with the present programme? Where is the demand? In what quarter of the country is there any demand to change the programme? The hon. member from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) has criticised the present arrangement very severely, and has said that it is a waste of money to spend two and a half millions on the five ships in commission. What will he say in regard to the million and a half the minister proposes to spend on the volunteer services, on the trawlers, and on the armoury' drill and the like? I have tried to find where the criticism of the present policy is. I fail to find it in the press. If there is criticism in the country, it .is that we are not doing enough, and that we reasonably should do more, but I have heard of no criticism inside the House or out of it, save only the words of the hon. member from Lunenburg, that the programme which we carried on last year and the year before should be at all reduced. Let the Government be content with that programme. I agree that it is not one of which we can boast very much, but it is infinitely superior to the programme 
which the minister brought down to the House earlier in the session. If the minister wishes merely to play at the naval game, let him form his naval volunteer force, and put out of commission these ships and his naval reserve. That is the scheme he has outlined, as I understand it, and to that scheme I am heartily opposed.

I
am sure the House has listened with a great deal of interest both to the statement made by the Minister of Defence (Mr. Graham) and also to the statement made by the hon. member from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), but it is very amusing to me, and I am sure it must have been to bon. members, to hear the hon. member from South Wellington speak about the "flop" which the hon. Minister of Defence had taken since last Friday. I presume that word flop comes quite naturally to the hon. member from South Wellington, because if there is one flopper in Canada to-day that deserves the title, it is the member for South Wellington. I need not go into details in order to explain to the House and the country how and why. The hon. member deserves that title, because everybody knows the whys and wherefores of what happened in 1917. The hon. minister has told us that he intends to keep the two destroyers, one on the Atlantic coast and the other on the Pacific coast, for training. I do not object seriously to keeping those two boats for training, but if, as his Director of Naval Service told him, the idea was to keep the vessel on the Pacific coast for the purpose of protecting the seal fisheries, it seems to me he is going beyond what is necessary in regard to this matter from a naval standpoint. In my opinion, the matter of protecting the seal fisheries in the Behring straits comes entirely under the Fisheries Department, and should be looked after by one of the Fishery patrol boats.
The matter of the Canadian Navy, as has been said by the hon. member from South Wellington, is one in which the people of the country have been interested for a number of years, but it comes, in my opinion, with very bad taste
5 p.m. from the hon. member from South Wellington to compare the record of the Liberal party in regard to their naval plan, either their past history or their present record, with that of the party with which he is now associated.

I made no comparison.

Supply-Naval Service

-or what happened the last few years in Canada in naval affairs. It might be well to review this matter in a very few words to show what both parties have done; in that way we can come to a conclusion as to whether the policy of the Liberal party, or the policy adopted by the Conservative party, is the better one. I have taken the trouble to look up the records of this House, in order to find what practical work was done by the government of this country previous to 1910 when the Naval Service Act was introduced, and I find that neither the Conservative government nor the Liberal government spent any money on what is known as the Naval Defence of this country. I need not go back very far. For instance in the year 1905-6, the year 1906-7, the year 1907-8, or the year 1908-9, there was not one dollar voted by this parliament towards the naval defence of this country. Although the hon. member from South Wellington says that I was the only person in this House who had criticised the navy and the naval expenditures, yet it seems to me that I should be more interested in the protection of the coast lines of this country than the hon. member for South Wellington or in fact any other member who lives in the interior of the country. I do not wish to say that they should not take an interest in this matter, but I think they will be the first to agree with me that those who live on the Atlantic or the Pacific coast are more vitally interested in the protection of those coasts than those who live in the interior of Canada. I remember during the years of the war, in the years 1918, 1919, when German submarines came across the Atlantic, when those submarines were within five miles of the Atlantic coast, we realized that it would have been very nice to have a navy. But we were not scared at all. The people who were born and bred on the Atlantic ocean are not so easily scared. The hon. member from South Wellington has said that I am the only one that has risen in this House and criticised the navy and deprecated the fact that so much money is being wasted, but it seems to me the members of the House and the people of the country will agree with me that I have more interest in the matter than the hon. member has in view of the fact that I live on the Atlantic coast, and represent an Atlantic coast constituency.
Neither the Liberal party nor the Conservative party spent one dollar on naval defence up to 1908-9. The Laurier naval policy was introduced in this parliament
in the year 1910. I need not tell hon. members what that naval policy represented or what it meant, but the Liberal party endeavoured at that time to put an act on the statute book and to carry it out, in order to create a naval sentiment in this country. Although the Liberal party voted in this Parliament for a naval service, and purchased from the Mother Country two training ships, the Niobe and the Rainbow, when the bye-election came in the county of Drummond and Artha-baska in 1910, the very gentlemen who are now supported by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), aided and abetted by certain Tory newspapers in Quebec-English newspapers at that- went through the country and did everything possible to defeat the Liberal candidate, purely and solely on the question of Canada's share in the naval defence of the country. That is what happened. And yet the hon. gentleman rises in this House and throws taunts across the floor, endeavouring to show that we on this side are not interested in naval matters in Canada. It is a well known fact that leading men in the Conservative party sent telegrams of congratulation to the Conservative candidate-more truly speaking, the Nationalist candidate-in the county of Drummond and Arthabaska, eulogizing him for the attitude he was taking in that campaign. Then what occurred when the general election came on in 1911? Did the Conservative party uphold the Liberal naval policy which was passed by this House in 1910? Did they go up and down the country telling the people that we ought to have a naval policy in Canada and that we should have ships on the Atlantic and the Pacific in order to protect the coast lines of this country and safeguard the avenues of traffic on the two oceans? Not at all. They did not utter a single word in favour of the naval policy in that campaign. On the contrary, the leading men of the party which the hon. member for South Wellington now supports toured the province of Quebec supporting the Nationalist candidates who were opposed to the naval policy of the Liberal party and of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. They told the people of Quebec that if Sir Wilfrid Laurier was elected and his naval policy was carried out their sons would be commandeered and carried across the seas to Japan, there to be disemboweled. And one of the men who conducted this sort of campaign was chosen as Deputy Speaker of the House, afterwards becoming a Cabinet Minister in the Conservative govern-



Supply-Naval Service
ment. That gentleman it was who gave utterance to the famous saying that in order to breathe the breath of freedom "it was necessary to shoot holes through the British flag." Yet these are the men for whom the hon. member for South Wellington is acting as spokesman, criticizing the Liberal policy with reference to naval affairs in this country.
What transpired after the election had taken place? They had to carry out their bargain with the Nationalists of Quebec, twenty-two of whom were returned to Parliament as a result of that campaign, which was one of the most dastardly campaigns ever carried on by a political party in Canada. Did they spend $2,500,000 in naval defence? Not at all. The Liberal party in 1910-11 expended $3,000,000 on naval affairs, and in 1911-12 they voted $3,000,000 again for the navy of Canada. But as soon as those gentlemen assumed office, to demonstrate just how much interest they had in the naval protection of our country on the Atlantic and the Pacific, in 1912-13 they reduced the vote to $1,600,000; in 1913-14 to $1,000,000; and in 1914-15 to only $1,000,000. Now, that is the naval policy they carried out. They had so little interest in naval matters that they reduced the vote in 1913 and 1914 by $500,000 more than the minister (Mr. Graham) is reducing at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: And that was before the war.

Yes, one and two years before the war. The two ships that were purchased from Great Britain, the Niobe and the Rainbow, were splendid vessels, admirably adapted for training purposes, and they could have rendered very valuable service not only before the war but even during the war. But the Conservative government did not keep the crews on these ships after they had made their bargain with their Nationalist friends. They paid off the crews, and the Niobe was tied up at dockyard at Halifax, with two chains at her bows and two at her stern; and there were not sufficient caretakers left on board to keep the machinery in order. When the war broke out in 1914 this boat was moored to the dock, grounded on her beef bones, and it took six weeks after the declaration of hostilities to get her into any kind of shape to go to sea. As I said before in this House, and I repeat it with emphasis on this occasion, if the Niobe had been put into commission on the Atlantic, and the Rain-

bow on the Pacific coast, on the 4th of August, and if the telegrams that came from the Pacific at that time had been answered-and it could have been effectively answered had these ships been in commission-there would have been a sufficient number of vessels captured on the Pacific and the Atlantic to pay the cost of the war to Canada for the first year. But these people did not want to do anything for the navy. The Borden government did not want to do anything for the defence of the country, and no other conclusion could be arrived at than that they were afraid to break the bargain which they had made with the Nationalists. The war went on and we spent a great deal of money-some $30,000,000-on what was described as naval defence. I have no hesitation in saying that most of that money expended during the war on the Atlantic and the Pacific was wasted. In 1920, the Union government accepted five ships from Great Britain. Now, the people of the country were not consulted in regard to that gift. I do not blame the British government for having offered these ships to Canada; indeed, I think they are to be commended for having done so. But I do say that the ships were accepted by the government of Canada without the authority of the people, who were not consulted in the matter. Notwithstanding the fact that Parliament was then in session, the whole thing was done over the heads of the people's representatives. Is there any man within the sound of my voice, or in Canada, who will assert that since these ships have come to Canada they have been of any practical value so far as the defence of our coast lines is concerned, or in keeping the traffic lanes open on either coast? I do not hesitate to say that they have been absolutely useless for defensive purposes. They have served no good purpose in the last two years, and whatever money has been spent to pay the crews and keep these vessels in commission has been utterly wasted to the people of this country.
Does the hon. member know what the British Admiralty are doing with the same kind of ships which they sent to Canada as a gift?

To use the words of the hon. member for South Wellington, they are "scrapping" them. I repeat that these ships, for purposes of defence at any rate, have been absolutely useless, and to prove that statement I have only to call atten-

Supply-Naval Service
tion to the fact that they have not spent three months on the Atlantic coast or on the Pacific since crossing the Atlantic. They have been wandering all over creation. They arrived in Halifax some two years ago, remained there about six weeks, and the first thing we read in the newspapers was that they were going to take a trip to the Pacific. They were fitted out at great expense to the country and proceeded down to the West Indies and through the Panama canal, and after a time we learned through the newspapers that they had arrived at Vancouver or Victoria. Now, that was a delightful trip. I have no doubt that most of us would have liked very much to be on board one of those cruisers or torpedo boat destroyers on such an extensive and delightful voyage. But I think every one will agree with me that that trip was of no practical benefit to this country. Those ships were not defending the Canadian coast line while on that trip, and consequently no one can argue that from the time they left Halifax for Vancouver until their return to Halifax two or three months later any practical results were obtained in regard to the defence of our shores.
Then during last winter did those ships stay on the Atlantic coast and do any par-1 ticular service that enured to the advantage of this country?-and I need scarcely add that during the winter months we can use boats of this description on the Atlantic coast, poor as they are, for the weather there is very rough; men of the merchant marine, both those in the liners which cross from the Old Country to Nova Scotia and those in the sailing ships which ply to all parts of the world practically, have to make that coast in stormy weather during the winter months, and there are times when it might be very handy, if a wireless were sent from one part of the coast to another that a ship was in distress, to have these ships available to render aid. But where were they when they might have been of some service? For four months those ships were down in Barbados and Trinidad. In fact the officers and crews helped to open the Barbados legislature.
The winter over, those ships are now back in Halifax. But what work is there for them to do in regard to defending our coast line or keeping open the lanes of traffic? I say those ships are absolutely useless. And the question in my mind is not whether we should continue these ships in commission, but: Can we in our present
117i
financial condition spend sufficient money for the upkeep of a navy which will not be of any service for our national defence either on the Atlantic or the Pacific, or to keep open the ocean lanes for our merchant marine? There is the whole question. Will any sane Canadian say that one cruiser, two torpedo boat destroyers and two submarines would be of any service if war broke out between Canada and- what country shall I say?

There is no country
with which we can possibly be at war.

I agree with my hon. friend, because we are a peace-loving people and are not going to seek an excuse for declaring war against any country. But if war did break out, what use would these five boats be to defend our coast line either on the Pacific or on the Atlantic? How would you subdivide them? Would you cut the Aurora in two and send one part to the Pacific coast and keep the other part on the Atlantic coast? The minister says that he is going to send one torpedo boat destroyer to the Pacific and retain one on the Atlantic. He can do that with those destroyers, and also with the two submar-1 ines. But what effective service could one destroyer and one submarine on either ocean render to this country? Absolutely none whatever.
My argument is the same to-day as it always has been-that if we cannot spend $100,000,000 a year in order to maintain a sufficient navy on both oceans to be ready for any eventuality, which is absolutely improbable, then it is useless for us to spend $2,500,000 or $1,500,000 for the purpose of pretending that we have a navy.
I do not think I need argue the point any further. There is the whole question in a nutshell. Many hon. members will recollect that when, two years ago, we were discussing the taking over of those five boats the then President of the Privy Council, Hon. Mr. Rowell, in reply to my contention that the ships were no good for defensive purposes, said: Oh, no, that is not what they are intended for. They are to keep open the traffic lanes so that shipping can move between the Atlantic and the Pacific with safety. And no less an authority than the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) supported the view expressed by the then President of the Privy Council.
No man who knows anything about marine matters will dare get up in Parliament or

What is the amount of
their naval estimates to-day?
I have not got that information.

That reduction does not
mean very much unless we know what the appropriation was before and what it is now.

I quite understand that that is a small reduction compared with the total naval expenditure of the British government, but I think it will be admitted that the very fact of that reduction being made proves that they realize the necessity for reducing their naval expenditure. Certainly if the British government feel justified in making that reduction, it seems to me that, as I said a moment ago, situated as we are, if we cannot afford to spend a sum of money that will give us something practical in the way of naval service, then it is good business for us to reduce our naval expenditure to a minimum.
I am very much afraid that whilst an overwhelming majority of people in this

country are not favourable to naval expenditures of any great magnitude, a small minority do not share that very widespread view. A few days ago I read a press dispatch from London of a speech made by Lord Lee, First Lord of the British Admiralty, in the course of which occurs the following:
Lord Lee pointed out that the Imperial Conference after a full, prolonged and intimate discussion of the naval needs of the Empire, had agreed that the maintenance of an Empire navy was the common concern of the whole Empire.
In other words, Lord Lee says that the delegates to that conference which was held in London last year agreed "that the maintenance of an Empire navy was the common concern of the whole Empire." So far as I am concerned, if that was agreed to by any delegates from Canada, I submit that they should not have done so without first consulting the representatives of the people in this House. It was bad enough for the then government to accept these five ships without consulting Parliament, which was in session at that time, but it seems to me it is worse for members of any government to go to the Old Country and agree with the British representatives and the delegates from the other Dominions that they would do something in regard to Empire naval defence without first consulting the views of our people through their representatives in Parliament.
As far as I am personally concerned, I am fairly well satisfied with the atatement made by the Minister of Defence (Mr. Graham). In view of the fact that we have some sort of naval organization, I think that perhaps it is not right or fair that the whole naval vote should be cut out at once. I can understand that it might not be necessary for him to spend the $1,500,000 which he is asking for, and I suggest that ir. the interests of the people he should save any part of that amount which he can as the year goes on.
As to the proposal of the minister with regard to arranging for naval service training for two or three weeks each year, I must agree with the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), that it is impossible to make sailors in two or three weeks. The hon. member said, in effect, that the money would be wasted in any attempt to make sailors in that short time.

Does the hon. member consider that a sailor can be made at all on one of these ships? In order to get the proper training, would the men not have

Supply-Naval Service
to go on sailing ships, square-riggers, and so on?

I think my hon. friend is right, to some extent. They do make sailors now on steam vessels, though they are not able seamen or as good as the sailors you make on square-riggers, fore-and-afters, and tern schooners. But I say you cannot make a sailor in three weeks. If the argument of the hon. member for South Wellington is good, that you cannot train a man for naval service by keeping him two or three weeks in an armory, on a training ship, or even by sending him two or three weeks to sea, either on one of these patrol boats or on one of these destroyers, then it seems to me the same argument should hold good with regard to the militia, and I am only sorry now we did not fight harder to get the militia vote for annual training further reduced. If you cannot make a sailor in two or three weeks, you cannot make a soldier in two or three weeks.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would succeed if he tried again.
In making a soldier, or a sailor?
No, in getting another reduction in the militia estimates.

I am a very modest man.
I will let the hon. leader of the Opposition read between the lines; he can come to his own conclusions. I believe, however, there is some merit in the proposal put forward by the minister in regard to a naval reserve. Some of the very best men who were in the British navy during the war, either on the fighting ships or on transports, were men who had been trained in the naval reserve. We all remember the gallant stand taken by the British army on the Gallipoli Peninsula. We remember reading in our newspapers one morning of the decision to abandon the peninsula. We read the vivid story of how these soldiers fought and backed their way down the hill fighting inch by inch, and when they arrived on the Gallipoli beach they found the boats there, ready to take them to the transport. We read that the sailors, naval ratings from the transports, were on the shore; they saw that the soldiers and their equipment were put on the transports. To the naval reserve was left the gallant task of firing the stores on the beach and being the last to embark; and these men had been trained in the naval reserve of England and the naval reserve
of the small dominion of Newfoundland.
If the minister, then, can work out some scheme whereby, at a minimum of expense to the country, we can train a naval reserve, the money will be well spent. I myself have a scheme in my head, Mr. Chairman, which would not cost very much money. We all remember that during the late war the Militia Department created a kind of sausage machine from which they ground out honorary colonels by the bushel. Now, I do not want the Minister of Defence to make me a rear-admiral for this suggestion, but I want to say this to him. We have on the Atlantic coast, and I think also on the Pacific coast, men who require practically no training; men who can be enlisted in a voluntary naval reserve at very small cost to the country. If the minister would like me to do something in this regard I could get anywhere from 5,000 to 10,000 volunteers in my own county to serve as a naval reserve on the Atlantic coast. These are the men who should be engaged; they do not have to be made sailors in two or three weeks, for they are sailors now. They have ploughed the seas ever since they were boys of twelve or fifteen years of age; they have gone fishing on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, and during the war they braved the submarines in the bay of Biscay and in the Mediterranean, carrying foodstuffs to the people of Europe. These are the men, who in my opinion, are ready to do either the work they did before, or any special work in connection with the defence of their country. It is not necessary to spend much money on a naval reserve this year; the minister should go slowly and work out a proper scheme, and not be in a hurry to spend any more this year. But if the time comes when the minister thinks it necessary after mature deliberation to have a naval reserve, I say that in my county-and in this respect it is only like a number of other counties along the Nova Scotia coast-thousands of young men can be obtained by the voluntary system who will be glad indeed to give two or three weeks a year, or more, in order to be so trained that they may be able to serve their country if necessary, in her defence.
In conclusion I may say that I should be very glad to vote any sum of money which I considered necessary for naval defence, either on the Atlantic or on the Pacific coast. But I submit that either $2,500,000 or $1,500,000 devoted to the naval defence is almost wasted, even though it is given the name of money voted for the naval
Supply-Naval Service

service. Let us be reasonable and sensible in this matter; let us look at it from the plain, business standpoint. If we cannot do anything in the matter of naval defence with either $1,500,000 or $2,500,000, then why should we be talking across the floor of this Chamber just because we feel we want to make some point against the Minister of Defence on the ground of his having cut down the estimate? I say he should be congratulated for cutting it down, and, further, that unless he can propose a good scheme under which it would be necessary to spend money on a naval reserve, the minister when he comes before the House another year would follow a course approved by the people, not only of the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, but of the country generally, if he said: "I find it is not a practical thing to spend money on a naval service, so I have decided to cut the whole thing out". I say the people of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific would give the minister credit for doing what he thought was right in the general interests of the country.

The hon. member (Mr. Duff) made the statement that one of the ships purchased by the Laurier government was chained to the dock at Halifax, by the late government when they came into power, and that the other was laid up at Vancouver. He said that if these ships had been in proper trim to go to sea when the war broke out they could have seized enough shipping to pay for the war.
No, I did not say that.
The hon. member said, if I am not mistaken, that if these ships had been ready for sea when the war broke out they could have seized enough shipping to pay for the first year of the war.
Yes, the first year. The hon. member said the whole war.
Then the hon. member said that so far as the five ships taken over by the late government were concerned, if war broke out they would be practically of no use.
I said, for practical defence purposes.

Would not these five
ships that were accepted by the late government serve a better purpose than the other two tinpot boats that were scrapped? Let us be honest. The five ships chat the late government accepted from the Imperial government, if they were in pr 'per

shape, would go a long way to defending at least the Pacific coast.
You can have them on the Pacific coast.

The hon. member for South
Wellington has said that he has not heard any criticism whatever of naval matters or of the grants to be made for the upkeep of the Canadian navy. I would like to say that there is a considerable body of opinion which has not been able to express itself through some of the Montreal and Toronto papers, which evidently are read by the hon. member for South Wellington. I would like to state further very frankly that so far as my constituency is concerned, I came here pledged to advocate national disarmament. That is not a personal viewpoint merely. It is the view of the people who sent me here, and I take it that the best contribution we can make in this House is to try to represent the opinion of the constituents who sent us here.
I quite agree that the expenditure of something like $1,500,000 on ships to defend the coast lines of Canada is a good deal like playing with the problem. I can quite appreciate the position that if you are really going to defend our coasts, you might rather have to spend $100,000,000. That is one thing that we should keep before us- the practical business side.
There is another aspect I should like to mention. We ought not to take any further steps in this matter until after the next Imperial conference and until after it is decided what the status of Canada really is. Some of us feel very strongly that we must not do anything whatever that would lead us into any sort of imperialism or draw us into responsibility for doing something over which we have not absolute control. We feel very strongly, a good many of us, that we ought not to be associated in any way whatever with any conferences which may possibly commit us to that from which we cannot very well draw back, but as to which we can have no final decision.
I am not at all sure concerning the reason for the acceptance of that gift of ships from the Motherland. I am not sure as to how much value they will be to this country. I happened to be in the city of Vancouver when that fleet came into English bay, and I know that a great deal was made in the papers of the event. It was suggested that this was indeed the

Supply-Naval Service
beginning of a real Canadian navy. The officers entertained and were entertained, and all that kind of thing, but there is a very large section of the people that since the Great War have ceased to be impressed by that kind of performance. It has been said on this floor to-day that the war is over, and yet there are members who have directed our minds back to 1910, and suggested that we ought to carry out certain policies which were proposed away back in that year. I submit that to-day we look out at the world with very different eyes from what we did in 1910. Surely the war has taught us some lessons, and among others that preparedness does not insure us against war, but that the surest way of creating and maintaining peace amongst the nations of the world is that we should indeed scrap our navies and our great armaments. You may laugh at such a position as that if you please. You may ridicule it; any hon. gentleman is at liberty to do that; but that is coming to be more and more the considered opinion of a considerable number of people in this, as well as in other countries.
Now that we have had a naval policy proclaimed at Washington, we are beginning to breathe a little more freely and feel that we can go on quitely with our business without undertaking any more of these tremendous financial obligations under which we have been labouring in the past. Surely we have an opportunity here in Canada of quitely reorganizing our affairs, not on the old basis, but on an altogether new basis.	[DOT]
The hon. member for South Wellington suggests that as the country grows, the naval service will grow and develop. That is precisely the militaristic point of view, according to which militarism is an essential part of any nation's life. Prom this standpoint we must always look forward to being able to defend ourselves by force of arms. I submit that that time has passed, that militarism is discredited, that the great world war, in which tens of millions of lives were lost and through which the whole world has been plunged into bankruptcy, has taught us that war is not effective, that militarism is a discredited weapon, and that we must look forward to the reorganization of our national and international affairs on an altogether different basis from that which we have had in the past. I would urge that we here in Canada very largely separated from other nations, and freer in that respect to work out our own affairs than most of the nations, should begin at once to stop naval expenditure and to recognize that it is only by the cultivation of international good-fellowship that we shall obtain any security from external attack.

Coming from a constituency which, in the days when shipbuilding was supreme in the province of Nova Scotia, built the largest wooden ships that were ever constructed in Canada, I feel it is my duty to rise and congratulate the minister upon a policy which will indirectly help in the very best possible way to bring back to Nova Scotia her commercial supremacy on the sea.
I was vgry much amused, as the hon. member for Lunenburg says he was, to hear the ex-Minister of Militia refer to "Hoppers." I am probably the youngest member in the House from the Maritime provinces, and while I have many sins to answer for, as I do not claim to be a paragon of righteousness, I am thankful that I do not have to answer to the atrocious charge of ever having been a "political flopper." I stand in this House this afternoon proud of the fact that I can support a Liberal Government, the true successor of the Liberal government led by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I followed the great Sir Wilfrid, as did all my forbears, and of him it can be said in the words of the poet Tennyson, he was a man "Who never sold the truth to serve the hour, Nor palter'd with Eternal God for power; ************
He never shall be shamed .. .what ever record leap to light.
I stand here this afternoon supporting my hon. leader who is the successor of that great chieftain, Sir Wilfrid, and whose naval policy has been vindicated time after time since he first enunciated it to Canada. He is not like the ex-Minister of Militia of whom we could say, as Sir Walter Scott said of "Old Immortality":
He delights in haunting ancient places and refreshing tombstones while the stream of life goes by and flowers bloom unheeded at his feet.
The hon. ex-Minister of Militia probably wants to get back to the days prior to 1910. Those were the days when my hon. friend had sound reasoning and peace of mind for he was standing for a policy which any reliable man in Canada would be pleased to uphold and advocate. But my hon. friend is sick at heart and has no peace of mind for he has shared in the vacillating measures which were adopted under the government of which he was a
Canadian Pacific

member, from 1917 down to the end of 1921. The result is, that in order to holster up a case against the excellent policy which has been enunciated by the present Minister of Defence he stands up and wobbles very much like a " land lubber " endeavouring to get his sea-legs while suffering from mal de mer caused by the bilge water from the pumps of the leaky ship of government which sailed Canada from 1917 up to December, 1921. We are not the only people that are making cuts in both military and naval matters. My hon. friend and colleague from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) has stated that Great Britain herself is cutting down her naval expenditure by eighty million? of money. The great dominion of Australia is also scrapping the Sydney, a ship, I believe, which was built wholly and entirely for Australia and of which Australians were proud. I believe that pursuant to the League of Nations an agreement was entered into looking towards disarmament, and we in Canada should not wait for the other portions of the British Empire to lead the way. We in Canada should not ask to be shown what other portions of the British Empire are doing in order to do the right thing, because Canada is mistress in her own house. Canada will be governed by Canadians; and I am proud this afternoon to know that we have a Government which has the courage of its convictions, a Government which will listen to the dictates of the Canadian people and also has the courage to see that Canadians shall be properly led with a view to economy not only in commercial matters but in military and naval affairs.
