House again in Committee on Bill No. 5, respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway Company-Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
On section 1-Extension of time for construction.

When this debate was adjourned I was speaking to the amendment offered by the hon. member from

Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). I am a member of the Railway Committee, but I was absent on the day this bill was considered, owing to illness-the only day I have been absent. Therefore, I feel that it is proper that I should be permitted to state my position in regard to this amendment. As hon. members will understand, this amendment, applies to six branch lines that are under charter to the Canadian Pacific Railway in the two Prairie provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Two of these lines are within the boundaries of the constituency of Battleford. My contention is that it is time that the railroad should show a disposition to begin to construct these branches, and that something positive should be required of this company. The country to be served by these branch lines in every instance is very much in need of this construction. Some of them have been in need of it, perhaps, for years. People settled along the proposed line. The war came on, construction was referred, and the settlers have gone on year after year at very great inconvenience.
The time has come, I think, vhen Canada should arouse herself from the lethargy in which she is resting to-day. If we propose to build up this country, it is time for us to get busy. I consider it almost a disgrace that at this time there should be unemployment in Canada. It is too bad that we should lack railway facilities at this time, when we have great need of improvement; when the world is in distress and needs those things which Canada can produce, and when people are hungry, cold and houseless. We have abundant natural resources, and great forests, but our mills are idle and our fields are uncultivated and uncut. Now are we going to get busy? What put Belgium back into industrial activity? Because she went to work. What must Canada do? Go to work. There is a job for every man who looks for one, if things are properly conducted in Canada. There is no excuse for unemployment. It is a crime for the able-bodied men in this country to go without work for six days in the week. A longtime ago we were admoni-ished that six days we should labour and do all our work, and on the seventh we should rest from our labours, because it is the Sabbath of our Lord. What does that mean? It means that we must observe the Sabbath, but it means a little more than that. It means that for six days we shall labour, and the man who loafs six days violates that commandment every day

Canadian Pacific
of the six, and if he loafs on the seventh, he violates that commandment also, for he is pursuing his ordinary avocation on the Lord's day. I say that in that command we have an assurance that every man can find a job if he looks for it, and I do not know where there are more jobs than here in Canada.
I do not know anybody in better shape to begin to employ labour than the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is laying away its surplus. The people are needing the extensions. The labourers require employment and the people need the money. Let us start the construction, and the railway will get the tonnage and the people will get service. The people will get something to eat, something with which to clothe themselves and the wheels of industry will start. Now is the time, just as quickly as we can get at it. If we stand with our hands folded year after year, and let things go by, it will only be a question of a very short time until we go into bankruptcy. We need immigration -in Canada. But we want something for them to do. We must improve the western part of the country if we desire to accommodate immigrants, and the way to improve it is to build branch railroads. We have plenty of trunk lines, but what do they amount to if there are no branches? It is the branches that bring business; they create the tonnage which makes the railroads profitable. I hope that hon. gentlemen will see the wisdom of providing that they shall go to work in earnest within two years and spend enough money to mean something. The Railway Act provides for an expenditure of 15 per cent, and that is the provision inserted in this amendment. I contend that it is a reasonable provision; otherwise the bill is substantially an extension of the charter for five years, and I do not believe that it is the intention that such an extension should be granted. I, therefore, sincerely trust that the House will see the wisdom of adopting the amendment.

This is the third time that this matter has been considered by this House. It was dealt with by the special committee, who granted the extension asked for; so I cannot understand why hon. members should persist in opposing it here. It has been discussed throughout the entire time devoted to private bills on each of the two former occasions it has been before the committee in this House, and the object has been simply to obtain, if possible, a snap verdict. Now, I believe in
the development of the country. But if I am rightly informed, as I think I am, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have seven or eight different branches in various stages of construction at the present time in the western provinces.* True, the Canadian Pacific Railway is a strong and powerful corporation; nevertheless, it is hardly reasonable or fair that it should be asked to do too many things at one time. The hon. gentlemen who have been insisting on this amendment are very loud in their protests against high freight rates. They demand cheap transportation. As I have just remarked, it is true that the Canadian Pacific Railway is a corporation of considerable magnitude, and hon. gentlemen say that they ought to be able to proceed with this work because they have all kinds of money. I do not dispute the fact that they have sufficient money for operating purposes; but neither the Canadian Pacific Railway nor any other corporation, big or little, using sound judgment, is going to take the money which it has for operating purposes and put it into permanent investment in the construction of roads. What they will do, before starting upon the construction of this or ony other important branch railway, is to go and sell bonds, and I presume there is not a gentleman in the House, who has had anything to do with the financing of any concern, who does not realize that the present is a very critical time to sell bonds to advantage. If we force the Canadian Pacific Railway to go and sell bonds for the construction of this extension, probably at seven or eight per cent and running over a period of twenty, thirty or forty years, we shall simply be putting a burden on them that will react on the freight rates. If I am correctly informed, the extension that has been asked for in this particular case can really be constructed only by the Canadian Pacific Railway. It can, of course, be built by the Canadian National Railways; but, for my part, the National Railways have as many lines on hand as they can operate advantageously, and I would not by any means advise that they should undertake to build any extensions that can be built by anybody else. The Canadian Pacific Railway are simply asking for the usual extension, namely, two years to commence and five years to finish. If the money market should happen to take a turn for the better and they could get their money reasonably, so that they could carry on the construction now under way, they would probably take advantage of the circumstance;
Canadian Pacific

because it is my belief that they are just as anxious tt>
build the extension as the people are to have it. The conditions, however, are such that it is not wise on the part of this Government to try to place burdens on the Canadian Pacific Railway or, for that matter, or any other corporation that would compel them to go into the money market and buy money at this particular time, when they would have to pay an extremely high rate of interest for it. In the interest of the western farmers and, indeed, of the people generally, who expect and want cheap transportation, we should give the railways an opportunity to take advantage of the money market when it is favourable, and when they can get their money at a reasonable price. I think the Canadian Pacific Railway has a record in this country that ought to be a fair guarantee that they are not bluffers or slackers, and that they will do their work and do it to advantage, if given a fair opportunity. It is not to the advantage of the western people, nor any other community in the country, that we should force the railways to go into the money market at an inappor-tune time, because if they have to pay too much for their money the cost will eventually fall upon the people in higher freight rates.

I want to say a very few words in regard to the bill, which is practically on a par with what I might term a sister bill' that was before the House a few days ago. Both of these bills -but I am speaking now more particularly of this one-were, I understand, fully considered and threshed out before the Railway Committee. Now, I do not wish to lecture the House at all, but I would observe that, with the large and well equipped committee which this House has for the consideration of private bills, such as the Banking Committee and the Committee on Railways and Canals, it would seem advisable, unless there is a vital principle at stake, that the decisions of a select standing committee should be accepted, for two reasons: In the first place, before that committee there appear the representatives of those who are interested. I understand, from the reports, that the Railway Committee gave this bill careful consideration. These very proposed amendments were considered by the committee, who decided to report the bill in its present form, or at least with the minor amendments referred to by the Chairman in reading the bill. In the next place, if we brought into the House these matters [Mr. McCrea.l
which are more or less in the nature of details, it would be desirable that the House should have before it in detail all the evidence and the reasons in support of or in opposition to them, just as in the committee. That is what should be done if the House is seriously going to consider from time to time minor amendments of this kind. Now, let us look for a moment at the amendments. As I understand the two amendments, one is to shorten the period of time from two years to one and from five years to three, for commencement and completion.
No.

Well, at all events, that is a matter of detail which the committee itself is more competent to determine than we are in this House, unless we are in a position to hear all the evidence. Now what is the situation? The section of the act which has been referred to by a good many hon. members-
The hon. member is not speaking to the amendment. He is speaking on the question of time, which is not mentioned in the bill.
I had passed from that and got to the question of bonds, so that my hon. friend's objection is not well taken.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The part of the bill which it is proposed to strike out reads:
-if within the said periods respectively the said lines are not commenced or are not completed or put into operation, the powers of construction conferred upon the company by Parliament shall cease, and be null and void as respects so much of the said lines as shall then remain uncompleted.
The point of time has some relevancy to this particular amendment, as the hon. member will see.

I so understood it, Mr. Chairman. In regard to such an amendment, the details are certainly more familiar to the Railway Committee than they are to this House, and if the House is to be called upon to determine all matters of detail after a bill has passed through the committee, then I consider we ought to have the same information as was furnished to the committee.
But let me turn for a moment to the question of bond issue. There is a clause in the Railway Act, inserted there a few years ago for a distinct purpose; it refers to the expenditure upon a railway or a branch line of a proportion of the capital

Canadian Pacific
stock or the bond issue of the railway company. That clause was inserted because we had a regular epidemic of railway charters. Individuals would get a charter for a railway, and then go out into the market and peddle it, hoping to secure some monetary advantage. This charter mon-gering, as it was called, became a veritable pest, so Parliament inserted in the Railway Act the clause to which I have referred. During the past few years that condition of affairs has almost, if not entirely, disappeared, and we have to-day but two great railway systems, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific-two enormous corporations controlling virtually all the railways of Canada.
This company and these branch lines are controlled by the Canadian Pacific Railway. There was only one criticism that I could direct at the application originally, and that has been taken care of by the committee, namely, the desirability of the Canadian National Railway having running rights over a portion of this line. That was provided for in the amendment now before the committee for adoption. So I think, Mr. Chairman, that it is desirable that we should accept the decision of the Railway Committee except where a matter of vital principle is concerned. I submit that in this case it is rather a matter of opinion after hearing all the evidence in the case which the Railway Committee had the advantage of hearing.
Let me take one further reference. In the course of this discussion some hon. members said that we should apply business principles in dealing with railway matters. We hear that opinion expressed very frequently, and in that connection from time to time the Canadian Pacific Railway is held up as an ideal business institution, which it undoubtedly is. But let us consider this point for a moment. The Canadian Pacific Railway with its enormous ramifications, and with its numerous railway extensions from year to year, cannot provide the necessary appropriations for those extensions in the same year in which it secures the bill for the purpose; it must plan a certain distance ahead. By the time this bill is passed a considerable portion of the season for construction will have passed, and in my estimation it is unreasonable, and has always been considered so, to ask any concern to commence operations within one year and to tie it down to that limited time with any sincerity of belief in its ability to fulfil the obligation.
I must say that this bill is satisfactory, both as regards the period of time and the bond issue, for these two matters are well cared for in the general act and in the method of procedure which has been followed so consistently in the past. Therefore personally I would feel very much disinclined to vote against the report of the committee which has given consideration to this matter after reviewing all the evidence.

In the Railway Committee I happened to be one of the supporters of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), and in the Committee of the Whole I also supported him, as I agreed to a great extent with what he was asking for. But this House has already twice defeated the motion of my hon. friend, and it seemed to me that on each occasion the majority of the members were in favour of granting this extension. Therefore why should we waste further time in endeavouring to hold up this bill? I have heard the matter debated pro and con, and I still have my own opinion in regard to it, but whilst I disagree with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) that this House should be guided by the report of the Railway Committee, I believe that the House should be supreme and that we should have an opportunity of discussing this bill if we deem it necessary.
Would my hon. friend permit me to interrupt him? I said we should be guided largely by the committee in matters of detail.

Yes. But this amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Al-berni having been twice defeated, I have only to say that although I voted for him on both occasions, I do not like this factious opposition, and as the majority of the House seem to be in favour of the bill, if the matter is pushed to a vote I shall reverse my former stand and vote for the bill.

I rise to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). I do not believe that any hon. members, unless they have had actual experience of western conditions, can appreciate what railway communication means to settlers in western Canada. We have spent many millions of money to induce immigration, and those who have come to this country have been guided to western Canada, and placed on government land on the assumption and
Canadian Pacific

the promise that railroad communication would be provided within a reasonable measure of time. Now, Sir, I can give from actual experience instances in some districts where the people have been ten, fifteen and twenty years on the land without railway communication, and they are anywhere from twenty-five to fifty miles from a railway. What use is it for this country to spend millions of dollars each year to bring in fresh immigrants when we have our old settlers leaving by the hundreds and thousands? I received a letter only the other day from a gentleman in my constituency to this effect:
If I have two thousand bushels of wheat to haul to the elevator this year, it will take me sixty days in the fall to do so.
You can readily understand that if you take sixty days out of a man's fall work there is practically no possibility of his making a success of farming where he is a long distance from the railway.
I am going to give the House two examples in my own constituency where the Canadian Pacific Railway have not kept faith with the people. Any one who is conversant with the southern part of Alberta knows there is a railway constructed from Lethbridge east to Manyberries. That line was supposed to join up the Canadian Pacific railway in Saskatchewan. Construction was started at both ends, but a section in the middle is not yet completed. In 1916, I believe it was, these two pieces of railway were brought within twenty-eight miles of each other, and the roadbed has been built on something like fourteen miles of that gap. There are 12 or 14 miles of road-bed to complete, and 26 or 28 miles of the steel have yet to be laid. The work, I believe, was done in 1916. You can understand how the settlers feel there, especially those who live at the eastern end of the portion which runs from Lethbridge when they have to pay on the hauling of their grain back to Lethbridge and then by Medicine Hat on the main line of the Canadian Pacific. The people on the other side of the Saskatchewan border who have to get coal from from Lethbridge may have to pay freight on their shipments all the way around from Lethbridge to Medicine Hat and Swift Current and back again to within 110 miles of Lethbridge. Now, I maintain that is a condition of affairs that should not exist and that the House should take into consideration. In the same constituency this company have for some years had a charter for the construction
of a road from a place called Leader in Saskatchewan to Pashley in Alberta. They built 25 miles of the line and this 25 miles has been running under construction for a number of years. Hon. members must realize that the construction company are running the trains over that 25 miles of railway, as the road has not yet been taken out of their hands; and the construction company in this ease, I believe, is the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. When any of the farmers in that district desire to use the services of this construction company for the hauling of a car of grain or other supplies a distance of 25 miles, the construction company charge them $40 or $50 for that service. It will be seen from these examples, therefore, that we in western Canada do not feel like letting bills of this kind pass without criticism. As a matter of fact, many of the members at this end of the Chamber were elected with a view to their protesting against this system which has been carried on in the past. We are here to protest against it, and that is what we are doing. * The time is not far distant when the railway companies which are getting grants of charters will be asked by the House to put up some bond guarantee as an assurance that the lines in question will be constructed within the time stated in the charter. I am satisfied that we have in the past been somewhat too easy in granting those charters and I believe the time is now ripe when the members of the House should see to it that these companies live up to their charters.

When an hon. member moved in this committee a few days ago to refer a bill back to the Railway Committee I supported the motion because the amendment had been moved in the committee itself, and I thought it was only fair that the bill be returned to it for further consideration. But the purpose of this amendment is to amend the bill in Committee of the Whole rather than to refer it back to the Railway Committee. The amendment has some merit; I am quite ready to agree with my ,hon. friends opposite who say that the railway companies are getting a little advantage over the act in this particular clause. But that matter also was discussed in the Railway Committee. I had it brought to my attention after the previous bill was placed before this committee that some hon. gentlemen who were opposing it did not understand that the particular clause which was in the bill had the effect of over-riding the

Canadian Pacific
Railway Act. But that circumstance does not occur in this case. My recollection is that no such amendment as is now proposed was moved in the Railway Committee. The clause was explained in the Railway Committee, and the committee adopted the bill as it is to-day-that is, with the amendment giving the National Railway the right to run over certain portions of the line. If this committee wishes to change the Railway Act or to over-ride the desires of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National in a clause which they want to insert in the bill, they have a perfect right to do it, either in this committee or in the House. But as the member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has pointed out, the railway companies, the people who are interested, cannot appear on the floor of the House and argue their point; therefore, I support the bill not as proposed to be amended in Committee of the Whole, but as reported by the Railway Committee.

Subsection (a) of section 1 of this bill affects the constituency which I have the honour to represent. The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) stated that this was a new charter. But this is not the case of a constituency in which the charter for the construction of a railway line has just been granted. I have a paper here from which I will read a heading in order to give you an idea of what the people of that constituency have been led to believe for years with regard to the construction of this line. The paper is dated at Edmonton, September 11, 1912, and it says:
Construction to commence at once on Bruder-heim-Whitford Lake Line.
Now, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are coming back to this Parliament and asking for an extension of charter. I may say that the announcement in this paper to which I refer has reference to the Canadian Northern, which previously had the charter. Owing to the subsequent financial condition of that road, however, they were unable to carry on and the government took the lines over; the Canadian Pacific then came along and secured a charter through this territory. In view of the fact that the Canadian Northern had the charter first, and in order to prevent duplication, a clause was inserted in that charter to the Canadian Pacific granting to the Canadian Northern certain running rights. The clause read:
Provided that for the purpose of avoiding duplication of construction on that portion of
the line west of Lloydminster, the approval of the route map may be made subject to joint construction or operation with the Canadian Northern Railway terms to be agreed upon by the companies or settled by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) tried to convince the committee to-night that the reason these railways were not being built was because of financial conditions. I have here a clipping, Mr. Chairman, dated March 1, 1920, in which the following statement of Mr. D. C. Coleman, of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was quoted:
The railway companies are very much concerned at the moment over the possibility of a shortage of suitable construction and track labour during the coming year, but if anything like an adequate supply of labour Is obtainable it is our intention to make a start on the Cutknife Northwesterly lines during the present year.
He made no statement as to difficulties on account of finances; he attributed them entirely to labour. I submit that the labour situation in the country to-day in itself constitutes an ample reason why the railways should start construction at the earliest possible date.
Now, referring back to that clause which has been inserted giving the National Railways and the Canadian Pacific joint running rights, I submit that is one of the reasons why the Canadian Pacific has held back the construction of this road. I have before me an extract from the Edmonton Bulletin of so recent a date as February 14, 1921, which also quotes some remarks made by Mr. Coleman. It states:
The obstacle standing in the way of the completion of the Cutknife branch, Mr. Coleman explained, was the fact that settlement had not been reached between the C.P.K. and the Canadian National in regard to the latters application for running rights, over the branch from Lloydminster to Whitford Lake. The vital importance of the completion of this branch to the people residing in the territory it would serve was pointed out to Mr. Coleman, who promised that everything would be done by him to bring the matter forward.
Now, I am satisfied the objection has been overcome. The Board of Railway Commissioners have sat and given their decision, and if the matter cannot be agreed upon in a satisfactory way it could be brought to arbitration and ultimately settled by the railway commissioners.
In the district I represent the farmers are hauling their grain from twenty-five to thirty miles and almost every hon. member on this side of the House has been petitioned for his support when this matter
Canadian Pacific

came before the House. I know the conditions with which the farmers there are confronted. It is one of the best farming districts in Alberta, and the Canadian Pacific have admitted that there is no deadwood in that line, but that it would be a paying proposition from the very start. I am not here to say anything against the Canadian Pacific. I think we ought all to be proud of what it has done. It has undoubtedly done a great deal for Canada, but at the same time I submit that it has been well paid for everything it has done. They are now asking for this charter. Well, there are always two sides to a bargain, and if the people of this country through their representatives in Parliament grant this company an exclusive right for a certain number of years to build that line of railway, then if another company came along to-morrow after this charter had been granted and offered to build a line of railway there, the Canadian Pacific would say, " No, you people are bound; you have given us a charter." I submit that it should work both ways, and that if the company gets an exclusive charter for a certain number of years, it should not be averse to putting up some guarantee or bond that it will carry out the undertaking.
I think the amendment is a very reasonable one. It does not curtail the time at all, but simply asks the company if it is acting in good faith that it will start construction within the specified time and*be prepared to spend a reasonable amount of money. I have therefore much pleasure in supporting the amendment.
Amendment negatived.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the course of the debate of last Friday, I made some very short comments on the Government's naval proposals, both as to their purpose and their extent, and by the sentiments I then expressed, though they followed immediately on the minister's address, I still abide. The minister to-day makes some alterations of importance as affecting some of the positions he took in his address of Friday; but as regards the general scope and purpose of his policy not of very great consequence. In the debate then, and now I am afraid, the Government will not have found among the hon. members of this House very much enthusiasm for its naval proposals. Of the hon. members who have spoken some are of opinion that the money voted, and the plans of the Government that the money is intended to realize, are such as to be of no value. Others oppose, because they do not believe in doing anything at all. The only thing there appears to be unanimity on, is that the money to be spent in accordance with the Government's plans will be wasted.
To get a comprehension of the question one does require to have in mind the history of this discussion in this Parliament and country for some years. The Government has not reviewed that discussion, although I think it should have. The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) has done so in a way; has done so in his way. I listened to him with interest, and there were some of his comments that were really worth noting. I thought, as he proceeded, that if he had not been so controlled by mad partisanship his common sense on this question wobld have had some show and might have triumphed.
The question arose first in this House in the session of 1909, when a resolution was proposed by Sir George Foster, now of the Senate. The debate I need not follow, for I do not want to be long. Suffice to say that owing to conditions, more or less serious, then existing, it was felt on both sides that unanimity was desirable, that possibly some sacrifices on both sides might

Supply-Naval Service
be made to gain it, and a unanimous decision was arrived at embodied in a resolution which I will not at the moment read but to which I will refer hon. members. It appears on page 3566, volume 2 of the Hansard of 1909. Summarizing that resolution, it said that Canada recognized her increasing obligation to take part in the common defence, of this Empire; that a system of periodic and regular contribution to a central navy was not the best system as a permafient policy; but that the House would approve of the creation-the speedy creation-of a Canadian naval service to meet the needs and purposes of the resolution. That was passed unanimously. The following year a Naval Service Act was brought into Parliament by the government of that day-a Naval Service, Act providing for the establishment of a Canadian naval service. Estimates for the purpose of carrying out that policy, aggregating, I think, the figures given by the hon. member for Lunenburg, $3,000,000, were introduced. The opposition of the day opposed that act. The opposition of the day took the ground that conditions had become more and more perilous; that it was evident we could not, under the terms of that act, develop such a trained force here in Canada as the act. contemplated, build such a fleet here in Canada as the act contemplated, within such time as would be effective at all to meet the world situation that was impending. Consequently, the opposition suggested that in place of commencing this policy now-without at all opposing it, on the part of its leader at all events, as the right principle for a permanent policy -instead of spending our money that way, under those conditions, we should spend it by way of direct help in order that Canada might do something in time of real assistance to the Empire in the trouble that was felt to be approaching. The government's bill passed. The government, I understand, advertised for tenders for the building of ships. I do not know when the tenders were advertised for: I think in July, 1910, because the bill passed early in that year; but the general election came on the 21st September, 1911, and no tenders whatever had been accepted. In a word, there was nothing done, save the marking of time, up to election day.
Following the election, an Imperial Conference was held, attended by representatives of Canada. The Admiralty laid before the conference certain facts tending +o show conference certain facts tending to show
the necessity of the whole Empire becoming sufficiently armed as to naval defence.
What year was that?

That was in 1912. The Admiralty, as well, laid before the representatives of the government of Canada, and of the Empire, certain additional facts which they did not feel could be made public but which were disclosed to the leader of the Opposition of that day. Upon those facts-based upon the public memorandum, and, as well, upon the undisclosed details-the government came to the conclusion that the only thing that could be done that would in all probability be effective would be to make then such effective addition to the central navy as would enable it better to meet the contingency that it was feared was only too clearly impending. No one contended even then that the war that later came was any certainty, that it was inevitable in any way; but the conduct of Germany was such that there was reason to fear danger in the not distant future. The government, therefore, proposed to Parliament the provision of funds to construct three capital ships, those ships to be owned by the Dominion of Canada, to be at the disposal of the British navy, subject to recall at any time by this Dominion, and to add to its effective fighting strength; and proposed that in the meantime-while we made that expenditure which was estimated to be in the neighbourhood of thirty or thirty-five million dollars-definite action for the creation of a Canadian naval service might well wait. We took that course. I was not a member of the administration, but the government took that course in the belief that only in that way could effective assistance 'be rendered in time; but the leader of the government at no time in his public career ever made any assertion hostile to the idea of a Canadian naval service as a permanent policy for this country.
The opposition of the day opposed that measure. The opposition moved an amendment-Sir Wilfrid Laurier moved it himself-an amendment which, along the lines of the resolution of 1909, admitted frankly the responsibility of this country, admitted our moral obligation to co-operate in the matter of naval defence, but set its words against the terms of the government's proposal, and1 proposed instead the creation of two fleet units-one on the Atlantic and one on the Pacific-under the Naval Service Act of 1910, in that way fulfilling, as they felt, the obligations of this country.
Supply-Naval Service

The arguments against that are the ' ones I have so very briefly set out, namely that it could not be done, the men could not be trained nor could the ships be built for the purpose, as it provided, in Canada, in any time that would likely be at all early enough to meet the emergency that was felt to be near. The government's policy was carried in the Commons and was defeated in the Senate. That debate was in 1913, and was perhaps the most momen-ous, from many respects, of any that ever took place in Parliament. In 1914, the year following, the war broke out. I am not making any boast as to the course the government pursued, it being vindicated by that war. If the war had never broken out, it would not have reflected upon the bona fides, nor upon the judgment of the administration. The fact is that the war did break out, and that if we had commenced in 1910 even, the creation of a naval service, under all the authorities that have had any experience in this matter, we could not have arrived at any effective service by the time the war did break out. Much less could we have done it if we had commenced in 1912 or 1914. However, in that position we confronted the struggle.
The next incident that took place of consequence was, I think, in the year 1918. I am not purposely omitting anything. I do not recall any consequential matter in the meantime. In 1918 the subject again came before the Imperial Conference. In that year the Admiralty presented a memorandum which I have not seen recently, but which, no doubt, is on record in this House, setting out the great advantages from a strategical standpoint of a central navy, and its great advantages, as well, from an economic standpoint. The representatives of the overseas dominions, however, felt that there were difficulties in the way of accepting the Admiralty's conclusions and putting them into realization in the * -'minions, because of strong local feeling there existing, and, as a consequence, there was presented to that conference, on behalf of the representatives of the overseas dominions, lay Sir Robert Borden, Prime Minister of Canada, a memorandum embodying the conclusions of those ministers. That appears in Hansard of the 27th of April, 1921. I have no doubt it appears sooner, but in the debate of that day it was quoted by myself, and may be seen in the speech that I made then. That was a debate on the subject of my duty, when I should go later to represent this country at the Over-

seas Conference. I think it is of sufficient importance that I read that memorandum to this House. It is at page 2640 and reads as follows:
The Dominion ministers, having considered the Admiralty Memorandum of May 17, 1918, on the Naval Defence of the British Empire, which was circulated to the Imperial War Conference, 1918, submit the following conclusions and observations:
1.	The proposals set forth in the Admiralty Memorandum for a single navy at all times under a central naval authority are not considered practicable.
2.	Purely from the standpoint of naval strategy the reasons thus put forward for the establishment of a single navy for the Empire under a central naval authority, are strong but unanswerable. The experience gained in this war has shown that in time of war a Dominion navy (e.g. of Australia) can operate with the highest efficiency as part of a united navy under one direction and command established after the outbreak of the war.
3.	It is thoroughly recognized that the character of construction, armament and equipment, and the methods and principles of training, administration and organization, should proceed upon the same lines in all the navies of the Empire. This policy has already been followed in those Dominions which have established naval forces.
4.	For this purpose the Dominions would welcome visits from a highly qualified representative of the Admiralty who, by reason of his ability and experience, would be thoroughly competent to advise the naval authorities of the Dominions in such matters.
5.	As naval forces come to be developed upon a considerable scale by the Dominions it may be necessary hereafter to consider the establishment for war purposes of some supreme naval authority upon which each of the Dominions would be adequately represented.
That as I said, was presented on behalf of the overseas dominions. The war, of course, not being at an end, no definite step was taken. A year ago last fall, the Prime Minister of Great Britain suggested a further Imperial Conference, or rather a conference of Prime Ministers. The telegram of invitation suggested certain subjects inclusive of the discussion of the wisdom of renewing the Japanese Treaty, and year following, was broke out. I am other matters connected with foreign policies. Subsequently the Prime Minister of Great Britain suggested further subjects among others, the question of naval, military and air defence. The invitation of the Prime Minister was accepted. A debate took place in this House on April 27, 1921, the government having fixed a day on Which members of the House might express freely their views as to what should be the course of Canada's representatives at the conference. In the course of that debate reference was made again to the memorandum I have just read, the terms of which,

Supply-Naval Service
upon the return of our representatives in 1918, were laid before the House, and as respects which, so far as my memory goes, there has been no adverse criticism in this Parliament. In the course of that debate the subject of naval, military and air defence came up. A motion was moved by the then leader of the opposition, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), embodying instructions to Canada's representative, that on no account was he to bind this country to any further naval or military expenditures. That resolution was resisted by the government on the ground that instructions to representatives at a conference were inconsistent with the very purpose and character of such an assembly; and that if that principle were followed by other countries, if their representatives were all to be shackled and bound in advance, then there would be no value in the conference. That resolution was defeated. In the debate I emphasized the view that there could not be any effective discussion of the naval question at that conference because, first of all, I was of the impression that the conference called was of the nature of a conference of Prime Ministers akin to the Imperial War Cabinet that had sat during the war, and that naval questions were more properly taken up at Imperial conferences proper, where matters affecting the dominions, in a domestic sense, came under review. Further, I expressed the view-and this was the argument which I emphasized repeatedly -that while the nations of the world were then groping, it was true, somewhat in the dark, but groping nevertheless, to come to some understanding by which the whole world burden of armaments could be reduced. I felt that until those efforts should have reached some fruition, and we would know what were to be the aggregate responsibilities thereafter of our Empire, we could not with advantage debate the question of naval defence. In the course of that conference, -though I am not at liberty to give the discussions, I am free to give the conclusions and such discussions as are revealed in the official document filed-a resolution was arrived at which, I may suggest, fairly well embodies the sentiments that I expressed in the debate in this House on the 27th of April preceding. That resolution I read to the House on Friday last. It is so pertinent that it should be read again.
That while recognizing the necessity of cooperation among the various portions of the Empire to provide such naval defence as may prove to be essential for security, and while
holding that equality with the naval strength of any other power is the minimum standard for that purpose, this conference is of the opinion that the method and expense of such co-operation are matters for the final determination of the several Parliaments concerned. And, second, that any recommendations thereon should be deferred until after the coming conference on disarmament.
Prior to the adoption of that resolution a prolonged debate had taken place on the renewal of the Anglo-Japanese Treaty. I may refer to a partial consequence thereof. Perhaps I should not use the word "consequence". Let me merely say that following the debate, after the debate, whichever way you choose to put it, the notable invitation came from President Harding for a conference on disarmament. That invitation was accepted with alacrity by Great Britain, following a most favourable reception at the hands of the conference itself. The disarmament conference, therefore, had been fixed, and in that way machinery was open by which there might be a consummation of the great longings of the powers that there should be some arrangement by which armaments could be reduced.
It is not out of place to interject here the observation that we get nowhere in these discussions by merely expressing an aspiration, a vague sigh and hope, that the nations may cease to do battle in the arbitrament of rights. We do not reach ou1 any distance towards armament reduction by merely throwing down our own arms and leaving ourselves at the mercy of those who do not. The sane nation, the wise nation, the nation that deserves the right to that appellation, seeks to the utmost of its powers, by coming to terms of agreement with other great nations of the world to make it possible, compatible with its own safety, to reduce its weapons of defence and then manfully carries the burden so reduced. That is the course which this Empire has pursued. I venture to say that of all the nations of the world, of this day or of any previous day, no one has ever struggled harder than has Great Britain, in the years before the war and in the years since, to bring about this much desired result. And of all the nations of this Empire there is none that has contributed more sincerely and ardently, and certainly -without the lightest thought of boasting-[DOT] more effectively than Canada has done to help the Empire towards that end.
The disarmament conference at Washington is the longest step that has ever been taken by the advanced nations of this world towards the practicable goal of dis-

armament. As a result of that conference, the possibilities outlined by the minister himself (Mr. Graham) in his speech of last Friday, have been arrived at. Great Britain is able to reduce her capital ships by, I think, twenty-three or twenty-four; and the United States, by the abandonment of projected vessels and vessels under construction, and by the scrapping of vessels prior to certain types, is also able to reduce her capital ship strength by, I believe, twenty-eight. The three great leading powers of the world, Britain, the United States and Japan-I do not omit France out of any feeling that she is not a great power, but her position is very much weakened by reason of the war, which we all undoubtedly deeply regret- came to a definite understanding as to ratio, an understanding which is the very heart and centre of the agreement arrived at,-that ratio being five, five and three in capital vessels, the complement or what might be termed supplementary vessels to be proportionate to the capital ships of each nation. That has been made possible as a consequence of the disarmament conference; therefore we know now the residuum, the aggregate responsibility for naval defence that rests upon the British Empire. We know now the point up to which we must go, and beyond which we cannot proceed. Therefore, we are in possession of the facts, to determine what are the duties of the Dominion in the premises, and what course it should pursue.
Now, the question arises: What is our duty? What is our obligation? Well, in the first place, I submit that we have an obligation. I do not know whether anyone disputes the fact or not. If anyone disputes it to-day, I am not aware of anyone who disputed it in April, 1909. The resolution unanimously agreed to in this House in 1909 acknowledged the obligation of this country. The very commencement of the resolution recited that obligation. But we do not need resolutions to enable us to understand our obligations. If in this world we receive the advantage of services rendered, it follows, I think, in the mind of. honest people, that we should contribute either to those services or to their upkeep. That we do receive to-day and have received through all our history the advantages of the British navy as a great public service, there is no room for doubt -no room for dispute at all.

The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) stated this afternoon that even in the late war, he, a citizen of Nova Scotia, residing on the Atlantic coast, had no fears at all. "Why," he said, "though the war raged around I sat there under my vine and fig tree and no man made me afraid." Why was that? The hon. member knows why it was. He rested in that security just for the reason that we all rested in the same position, just for the reason that many of the nations of this world, wholly independent of the British Crown, rested in like security-the reason being the strength, the power and the purpose of the navy of Great Britain.
While Canada was a growing nation we made no effort whatever to assist in that form of defence. We accepted the results with the feeling that we had some obligation to bear a share. But that feeling did not bring practical results; it was a matter of growth, of continuous and increasing realization, and the formal acknowledgment came in the resolution of this Parliament unanimously passed in 1909. Consequently we recognize the obligation. We do not recognize it as a contractual obligation ; it never was, it is not such to-day. We recognize it as a moral obligation binding upon us.
The method by which we fulfil that obligation, whether by co-operation through the construction and manning vessels of our own, or by assistance to a central navy- is for the choice of the people of this country through their Parliament in the light of the best opinion we can gather. The method is for us to choose, the extent we are to go is for us to choose; always it has been so, it is so to-day.
There has been difference of opinion as to what method we should follow; there has been difference of opinion even dividing parties in this House, but on the part of Canadians worthy the name and regardless of party there has been no difference of opinion as to the obligation itself.
Now, I venture to suggest that with that obligation existing, we cannot do justice to our own people, we cannot do justice to the manhood of this country, we cannot do justice to the children of this country, if we as a nation lie under a manifest moral obligation and refuse to do anything towards its discharge. The nation that plays the part of a poltroon and sponger in the life of the world will find that conduct reflected in the moral character of its people and in the estimation in which it is held abroad.

Had it not been for the belief in the imminence of war I do not doubt at all that this country would without serious party division have come to an effective conclusion as to the right line of naval policy. The belief in the imminence of war, and the difference of opinion that that involved, had the effect of severing us as to the best method to be adopted. Now that the war is past and we are in a position to lay down the lines of a permanent policy, the reasons for that division have disappeared.
We have now passed every emergency that then threatened us, but that there is no possibility of any future danger surely those who profess the truth will not contend. When we see Britain taking upon herself the obligation she does; when we saw the United States, prior to that conference, entering upon a squarely designed programme to surpass all the nations of the world; yes, when we see France to-day, even by the press of to-night bringing down a programme of naval construction and maintenance, exceeding by $69,000,000 her programme of last year, it begins to dawn upon us that we may be a little premature in concluding that the great new social order has arrived, and that the possibility of war has gone.
The duty of this country to-day is to devise a method of carrying out its just obligation in the light of existing conditions, and the question before this committee is whether or not the proposals of the Government fulfil this obligation. I purpose to inquire very briefly whether they do or not.
It is necessary to say first, that after the war in 1920 the ships that we had during the war were manifestly unsuited by that time for any purpose at all. I do not wish to enter into any controversy now as to the value of the ships that were bought in 1910-the Niobe and the Rainbow. It would not be inconsistent with argument ot assume that they were of some value then, but, they were of no value in 1920, and even long before that year-that is, of no practical value as a nucleus for a navy, and virtually of no value even for training purposes. So putting aside matters of controversy that do not affect the issue now at all, let us come to 1920. Feeling that we necessarily must commence some training, knowing what the other dominions of the Empire were doing, knowing what the Mother Country was doing, we accepted from Great Britain a free

gift, not of obsolete vessels at all, but of oil-burning vessels of the most modern type. We accepted the Aurora, built in 1914, an oil-burning cruiser; then we accepted two oil-burning torpedo destroyers, built in 1916, and two submarines, built either then or later.
I do not say there was an express undertaking with Great Britain, but as a matter of deliberate policy for ourselves we undertook to utilize those ships and to train upon them as best we could the personnel of a navy for this country. We undertook that and no more, because we felt that the time was coming, either through the League of Nations or otherwise, when the great powers would be able to agree to a reduction of armaments and thereby we would know what the obligations of the various nations were to be.
We started in this way, completed the complement of those vessels, and proceded to the work of training our young navy. The hon. member for Lunenburg endeavours to make fun of that navy. He says, " What use were those boats for guarding our seas? Why they took a trip down through the Panama canal and cruised around the west coast of Canada. They were not guarding our shores at all." He seems to think they were only utilized for joyrides for the seamen, or as spectacles for our population to gaze upon.
Now, let me put it to the hon. member for Lunenburg: Shores need to be guarded when they are attacked. Men need to be trained upon their ships when there is no attack-trained in time of peace for the purpose of meeting peril if peril comes. Does the hon. member think that the Royal Navy of Great Britain is strung around the British Isles watching for some hostile ship to fire a shot? Is the United States navy stationed at some short distance from the shores of that country, the ships a few flags apart, watching there for fear some hostile vessel may steam upon her shores? That is not what their navy is doing. Those navies were doing just what the navy of this country has been doing. They were training, they were steaming; they were proceeding to various portions of the world. The United States navy was doing that; the Royal navy does it continually. And I say this, without having looked at the records very lately -but I say it with considerable confidence: what we did was under recommendation as a good and effective way to serve the purposes for which the navy existed.

Now the minister in his address the other night expressed more than once his belief in the necessity of reduction consistent with safety and with national dignity. Mr. Chairman I do not stand as much on national dignity as some men; I would have been fully satisfied if the minister had stopped with "consistent with safety". When a nation has armaments reasonably consistent with safety, then there is consistency with national dignity, at all events to suit me. When you go as far as necessary for safety under world conditions you have gone all the length you need go for the purposes of national dignity.
Britain feels that for the purposes of safety she must maintain, a singlepower standard. She cannot afford to go below it. To do so-and she was recognized by all the nations of the world at Washington as being right in her decision not to go below a single-power standard-to do so she is called upon to expend in the neighborhood of $400,000,000. That is the position Great Britain is in. Great Britain be it remembered, until a very few years ago, being an island Empire, having responsibilities in every part of the globe- here and in the Southern seas and all over the world-Great Britain felt that in her peculiar position she could not be safe under less than a two-power standard. She was compelled to abandon that position some years ago. She adopted a 60 per cent defence standard-that is, over the next highest power, but for reasons good to her-doubtless owing in the main to the destruction of the German navy, Britain receded from that resolve and adopted a one-power standard. I am sure there is no citizen of Canada, there is no citizen of the dominions of the Empire, who would for one moment question the claim on the part of Great Britain that it is absolutely essential for her security that a one-power standard be maintained. Is Britain, in a naval sense, to pass to the standing of a second rate power? If she does, are we not affected just the same as the people
