But British connection is of value and something to be proud of if we rise to its responsibilities, as well as accept its advantages. There are those who say, "Oh, we are in favour of British connection because of the traditions of Great Britain, because of this and that other glory of Great Britain", but who follow by the assertion that we cannot pay any money in discharge of the responsibilities that undoubtedly are incident to British connections, responsibilities far less than we would have had to discharge if we stood independent as a nation-far less than our corresponding obligations would be as an independent nation. "Oh" they say "if we do anything in the way of assisting, in national defence, that is Imperialism" and they turn in holy scorn from the very thought of "Imperialism". But they say "nevertheless though we do not do anything we want British connection", and they call that loyalty. That definition of loyalty I do not understand. I do not argue that we as a Dominion ought to assist on a scale commensurate with our population, either by way of service of our own, or assistance in any othre form. Great Britain has responsibilities in respect of crown colonies, and I do not think there are any anyway who would not acknowledge that her responsibilitiy per capita is justly greater than ours. Surely on the ether hand no one will urge that 17 cents per capita for the Canadian people is fair assistance on our part, when the burden resting on England is something like $10 a head for the people of that country. I oppose the minister's proposal on the score, first in view of the plan he has revealed, and on the score that it is incompatible with the maintenance of the honour and self respect of this Canadian nation as an integral part of the Empire.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My right hon. friend who
has just resumed his seat has said, and I think quite rightly, that this question cannot properly he appreciated without some review of the history of the naval policy, and of the discussion which has taken place in regard to it. He says that the Government had not reviewed the discussion, though he thought they should have. I hope my right hon. friend did

not feel that, after he had sat down, the last word would have been spoken, because, while he did review the discussion to a certain extent, he left some material parts untouched. Possibly, I may find it necessary to review this question a little more at length than would have been necessary had my hon. friend not sought to have the House believe that he was covering all aspects of it. He very properly went back to the resolution of 1909, which was unanimously adopted in this House as the basis of the naval policy. He said he would not read the resolution to the House, but would quote the substance of it. I noticed in his quotation a particular phrase, whether it had any significance or not I could not say, but I doubt if it will be found in the resolution itself. It Was to the effect that this Parliament recognized an obligation in the nature of the common defence of the Empire. That was the expression he used. I am not saying whether that obligation exists or not, but I shall read the exact words of the resolution so that the House may have its exact terms before it. The resolution reads:
The House fully recognizes the duty of the people of Canada, as they increase in numbers and wealth, to assume in larger measure the responsibilities of national defence.
The House is of opinion that under the present constitutional relations between the mother country and the self-governing dominions, the payment of regular and periodical contributions to the Imperial treasury for naval and military purposes would not, so far as Canada is concerned, be the most satisfactory solution of the question of defence.
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of a Canadian Naval Service in co-operation with and in close relation to the Imperial Navy along the lines suggested by the Admiralty at the last Imperial Conference and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the Empire, and the peace of the world.
The House expresses its firm conviction that whenever the need arises the Canadian people will be found ready and willing to make any sacrifice that is required to give to the Imperial authorities the most loyal and hearty co-operation in every movement for the maintenance of the integrity and honour of the Empire.
That was the resolution accepted unanimously in this House, providing for the establishment of a Canadian naval service, and setting forth that whatever might be done in connection with the Canadian naval service should be in close relationship with the British Admiralty, and along the lines of decisions that had been reached at an Imperial Conference. The outcome of that
Supply-Naval Service

resolution was the act respecting the naval service, which was assented to on May 4, 1910. I have a copy of that act in my hand, and looking it over I think I am right in saying that it has in view four main objectives. The first is the provision for a Department of Naval Service and the administration of that department. The second makes provision for a naval reserve force. The third makes provision for a naval volunteer force, the organizing and maintaining of a force to be called the Naval Volunteer Force. The fourth provision, which is an important one, is that in times of emergency the naval service and the members of the naval forces I have spoken of may be placed by the Governor in Council at the disposal of the British Admiralty. That was the law passed in May, 1910, by the then Liberal administration. That law embodies the Liberal policy as it was stated at that time, and as we are standing for it to-day. There has never been a party which had greater reason to feel proud of its policy, more able to say that its policy had been vindicated by the facts of history at every turn, and that it was a wise and prudent policy in every particular, than the Liberal party in regard to its naval policy.
My right hon. friend said that after the Naval Service Act had been passed the Liberal party, in other words, the Government of the day, had done nothing save the marking of time, up to election day.
Two ships, the Rainbow and the Niobe.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Let us see
about the marking of time and make a comparison based upon facts as to what was done. Here is the record of the Liberal Administration while in power. The Naval Service Act was passed on May 4, 1910. Immediately, a deputy minister of the department was appointed, and steps were taken to organize the department in its different details. On the 8th July advertisements were inserted in the leading newspapers of Canada for the construction of vessels for the Canadian navy. Canadian and British firms were invited to tender. On August 18 the second-class cruiser, the Rainbow, which had previously been purchased by the Canadian government from the British Admiralty for use as a training ship on the Pacific, sailed from England and arrived at Esquimalt on Nov. 7.	On October 10 the first-class
cruiser Niobe, previously purchased from the British Admiralty by the Canadian

government for use as a training ship on the Atlantic sailed from England and arrived at Halifax on October 21.
Recruiting for both the Rainbow and the Niobe started on their arrival, also the organisation of the dockyard at Halifax. According to the report of the Deputy Minister of the Department of Naval Service for the year ending March 31st, 1911, recruiting was satisfactory and the complement of the Niobe was practically complete on that date. There were still a few vacancies on the Rainbow. By January 19th the Naval College at Halifax was formally opened. On May 1st, tenders, in accordance with the advertisement and information furnished, were received by the government of Canada from several firms. On May 12th, the Hon. L. P. Brodeur, Minister of the Department of Naval Service, sailed for England to attend a subsidiary conference of the Imperial Conference on Naval Defence. On June 29th, an agreement was concluded between the British Admiralty and representatives of the Dominions of Canada and Australia, respecting the control of the naval service and forces of the Dominions of Canada and Australia, setting forth the limits of the Canadian and Australian naval stations respectively. On July 16th, the Hon. Mr. Brodeur, returned to Canada. Then on July 29th, the Canadian Parliament was dissolved and on September 21st the Dominion general elections were held.
Because of the impending elections, the Prime Minister of the day, (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), with the high sense of honour that characterized him, felt that it would not be proper to accept the tenders and award the contracts immediately on the eve of the contest.
When were the tenders asked for and when were they received?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The advertisements were inserted on July 8th, 1910, and tenders in accordance therewith, based upon information furnished in the interval, were received on May 1st of the following year.
And the House was not dissolved until well en in July?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. But, as I mentioned, the Minister of Naval Defence was absent in England in the interval attending a subsidiary conference of the Admiralty on the question of naval arrangements.

Wrhen did he leave?

Supply-Naval Service

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He left on May 12th and returned on July 16th. I think the Prime Minister was also away at the time. He returned on July 16th and on the 29th of that month Parliament was dissolved.
Mr. MEIGHEN-: Why was the space of ten months necessary before tenders were received? And why were they not accepted when received?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My right hon. friend may know that, in regard to ships of this character, much of the information that had to be supplied to the firms tendering was necessarily of a confidential nature. It was furnished in part by the British Admiralty and, in part, from other sources. It therefore required considerable time in order to prepare the tenders for submission to the government. The position, as outlined indicates that if a government had tried its best to proceed quickly, and had eagerly sought to get the naval service under way, it could not have been expected to proceed much more rapidly than did the Liberal administration of that day. The Naval College had been established and the Naval Service Department brought into being. The tenders for the various ships were in, and the whole arrangements were virtually complete. But for the fact that the question of Reciprocity reached such an acute stage during the discussions of that year, the whole naval service would have been launched in the course of the year 1911. Was that marking time, as my right hon. friend suggests? That was doing everything it was possible for a government to do to bring into effect the original purpose of the act, that of creating a Canadian naval service.
But from the moment after the election of 1911, what happened? From that hour until the war was over, during all those years, the government that succeeded the Liberal administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier has not a single act to its credit. Although they came into power in 1911, and had before them the tenders for these various ships, they refused to award a single contract. That is how much attention they paid to naval service and how much they believed in the existence of an emergency. The Niobe and the Rainbow, for which sailors had been recruited, were tied up to the docks. If those hon. gentlemen believed in an emergency and were prepared to meet it in that way, they were not fit to hold office as the governors of the country. That is the difference between the two administrations. It is all very well to talk a great deal and to utter an abundance of words. But actions speak louder than words, and if the two administrations are to be judged by their actions, the country will not have much difficulty in deciding which of them prepared in an effective way to meet our national obligations in regard to naval service.
I will not follow my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) in his endeavour to arouse prejudice and passion in the country. It seems to be one of his weaknesses that it is impossible for him to make a speech of any length without injecting into it, sooner or later, something calculated to stir up racial or religious animosity in the country. But when he begins on this occasion to talk about Bourassaism as being a factor in any naval question before Parliament he is going pretty far afield in his effort to arouse prejudice and hatred, which we had all trusted were buried ere the close of the great war. I tell my right hon. friend that his time would be better employed, when he is talking about moral obligations-
May I ask my right hon friend-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Have I hit the right hon. gentleman again?

My hon. friend has a perennial joke on that subject. I suppose he may say that I am hit when I rise to refute a misrepresentation. The only method he has of hitting me is to misrepresent my position. Will he explain how the mention of Bourassaism is calculated to arouse prejudice and religious ill-feeling in the country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Fortunately I may leave the matter in the hands of the House. Hon. members are quite able to judge the effect and intent of my right hon. friend's remarks. I do not seek to misquote him in any way. However, I shall not go into the nature of the conflict in 1911. But I can remember how he and his friends in the province of Ontario went up and down the back concessions declaring that Laurier's creation was a tin pot navy. They told the people that he was a French-Canadian and would do nothing for the Empire; and while they were making these representations in one province, other of the right hon. gentleman's friends were going up and down the province of Quebec
Supply-Naval Service

saying that Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his party were too imperialistic, and were trying to force Canadians, by conscription, upon warships in order that they might be brought into European and Japanese broils.
My hon. friend may refer to others, but he should do them the justice of quoting them exactly. So far as I am personally concerned, I deny absolutely that I ever in my life-
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen opposite have the habit of meeting argument with roars. Now, I never made any reflection in my life on Sir Wilfrid Laurier or any other man because he was a French-Canadian. But I do not refrain from referring by name to any man as a political force merely because of his race.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My right hon. friend as the leader of a great party should be more chivalrous to his followers. He should be prepared to take upon his own shoulders the obligations of his party instead of always trying to creep out from under himself. I will not follow him in the history of the campaign of 1911. We all recall only too vividly the Nationalist-Conservative alliance whereby the Government formed in 1911 was composed of a certain number of Nationalists and Conservatives, which two forces operating together, prevented any step whatever being taken towards putting into force a naval programme to meet the obligations of the day, notwithstanding that those same hon. gentlemen were professing that there was a great emergency of which account should at once be taken.
In 1913 the government of Sir Robert Borden did bring into the House a resolution in regard to the navy. I shall read that resolution and the amendment which was proposed to it, and I shall ask the House to decide which of the two parties was the sounder in its judgmenton matters of naval policy. This is the resolution which was moved by the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden on the 5th December, 1912:
Resolved that it is expedient, in connection with the bill now before this House, entitled an Act to authorize measures for increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire to provide:
(a)	That from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada there may be paid and applied a sum not exceeding $35,000,000 for the purpose of immediately increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire;
(b)	That the said sum shall be used and applied under the direction of the Governor-in-

Council in the construction and equipment of battleships or armoured cruisers of the most powerful and modern type ;
(c)	That the said ships when constructed and equipped shall be placed by the Governor-inCouncil at the disposal of His Majesty for the common defence of. the Empire-
The phrase used by my right hon. friend a few minutes ago.
(d)	That the said sum shall be paid, used and applied, and the said ships shall be constructed and placed at the disposal of His Majesty subject to such terms, conditions and arrangements as may be agreed upon between the Governor in Council and His Majesty's Government.
The Liberal party opposed that particular policy as outlined. Why? Because they believed at the time that it was not as good a policy, for dealing even with the situation then forecast by the right hon. leader of the government of the day, as was the Liberal policy of 1910.

Which claimed
there was no emergency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will answer my hon. friend in one minute.
I ask the members of this House to appeal to the events of history as they have transpired, since that resolution was proposed, and ask themselves how far the judgment of the then Prime Minister was to be compared with the judgment of the leader of the Liberal party of that day.
What was the proposal? To give to the British government a contribution in money for the construction of three of the largest battleships in the world. That is what was then proposed. Of what service would those three battleships have been in the late war? The large dreadnaughts were of little or no service and supposing that resolution had carried, what would be the situation as regards those ships to-day? They would have been in British waters throughout the whole period of the war without being of any real service at all, and to-day they would have been among the number of capital ships consigned to the scrap heap. Does my right hon. friend think that that judgment was sound and safe and calculated to ensure permanent support for the Mother Country and a fuller recognition by this country of its obligation in the matter of naval defence?
But what were the facts in regard to those ships; why was that proposal made? It was made because of the Nationalist-Conservative alliance, so that the Nationalists in the government might go to their friends in the province of Quebec and say, "We are proposing to give a contri-

Supply-Naval Service
bution of money to England to purchase three of the largest battleships in the world, and so end for all time to come anything in the nature of a Canadian naval service or a further recognition of our obligations." And in order that the Conservatives in the government might go to their Imperial friends in the province of Ontario and say, "This is only the first step in a series of contributions towards a permanent Imperial naval defence fund." That was the position.
Is the hon. Prime Minister not afraid that by attacking the Nationalists of Quebec he may arouse race and creed divisions in this country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am not in the least afraid of arousing any prejudice in that connection. If my right hon. friend is still sensitive in regard to his Nationalist allies, I feel sorry for him, but I do not think there will be any danger such as he suggests from any remarks I have made.
Now may I quote what was proposed in the amendment to this resolution of the government of the day? The Liberal amendment was wholly consistent with the Liberal policy as laid down in 1910; and, let me repeat it again, in the light of the events of the war it has been vindicated and justified a thousand times over. The amendment proposed was as follows:
This House declines to concur in the said resolution and orders that the same be referred back to the committee, with instructions to amend the same in the following particulars, namely, to strike out all the words after clause (a) and substitute therefor the following:
The memorandum prepared by the Board of Admiralty on the general naval situation of the Empire and communicated to this House by the right hon. the Prime Minister on December 5th shows that several of the most important of the foreign powers have adopted a definite policy of rapidly increasing their naval strength.
That this condition has compelled the United Kingdom to concentrate its naval forces in home waters involving the withdrawal of ships from the outlying portions of the Empire.
That such withdrawal renders it necessary that Canada without further delay should enter actively upon a permanent policy of naval defence.
That any measure of Canadian aid to Imperial naval defence which does not employ a permanent policy of participation by ships owned, manned and maintained by Canada and contemplating construction as soon as possible in Canada, is not an adequate or satisfactory expression of the aspirations of the Canadian people in regard to naval defence (and is not an assumption by Canada of her fair share in the maintenance of the naval strength of the Empire).
This House regrets to learn the intention of the Government to indefinitely postpone the carrying out by Canada of a permanent naval policy.
It is the opinion of this House that measures should be taken at the present session to give effect actively and speedily to the permanent naval policy embodied in the Naval Service Act of 1910 passed pursuant to the resolution unanimously approved by this House in March 1909.
This House is further of the opinion that tq increase the power and mobility of the Imperial navy by the addition by Canada under the above act of two fleet units, to be stationed on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of Canada, respectively, rather than by a contribution of money or ships, is the policy best calculated to afford relief to the United Kingdom in respect to the burden of Imperial naval defence, and in the words of the Admiralty memorandum, to restore greater freedom to the movements of the British squadrons in every sea and directly promote the security of the Dominions; and that the Government of Canada should take such steps as shall lead to the accomplishment of this purpose as speedily as possible.
There was the Liberal position in December 1912. Though the government of the day had wasted two years, though they were talking emergency and had let two years go by without doing anything, that was the course the Liberal party in this Parliament urged they should immediately adopt, and in which course they would have had the support of the Liberal party, namely to construct as speedily as possible fleet units on the Atlantic and on the Pacific coasts.
I ask my right hon. friend, I ask any other member of this House, if that course had been followed as was suggested by the Liberal party in 1912, would not this country and would not the British Empire have been in a much better position when war came in 1914-would they not have been in a position to deal more effectively with the situation that then developed?
But my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) said something a moment ago about an emergency. To show how insincere the then government was, in regard to its proposed construction of dreadnaughts to meet any emergency, when the bill passed this House-as it diil under closure in that momentous debate to which my right hon. friend referred,- and went over to the Senate, it was defeated there, as he has already stated. But what did Sir George Ross, leader of the Liberal party in the Senate, say at the time of that defeat? He pointed out very clearly, that the only reason the government was proposing this contribution of dreadnaughts by a separate act was, that the Nationalists of Quebec might tell their followers there, that it was a means of escaping any permanent naval service, of getting rid of it entirely and of any obligation under it; and Sir George

Supply-Naval Service
made this statement in the course of the debate from which I now quote:
Under the Laurier Act of 1910 now in force any number of millions could be contributed by Parliament if so disposed. Why then harass Parliament with a bill which is not required for emergency purposes and which is not as effective as the Act of 1910? If the hon. gentlemen are sincere in their efforts to meet an emergency, let them withdraw the bill now before us, and submit to the House a supplementary estimate for ten or fifteen millions for the speedy construction of battleships, wherever they can be built and then, from year to year, ask parliament for such additional sums as may be necessary for their completion, according to the practice of parliament in regard to all larger appropriations.
I do not know that a single senator would object if it was proposed, in the regular and parliamentary way, to do that. May I say more: the bill provides that this money shall be applied in the construction of a certain number of ships. That could be done under the act of 1910. I am informed that it is the indention to construct three battleships under this bill. If hon. genlemen or the government of the day wanted four or five they could build them wherever they pleased under the act of 1910.
Now, what has my hon. friend from Oxford to say about the belief in emergency under these circumstances, and the Government's endeavour to meet it?

On January 19',
1914, a year before the war, the Liberal party took the ground that there was no emergency-even at so late a day as that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am stating the position the Liberal party took in this Parliament, the position that they maintained consistently from 1910 until the moment of the war. It was that this country should construct fleet units on the Atlantic and on the Pacific, and should do so just as speedily as possible; that there was legislation on the statutes to enable any government to do what it pleased in the way of constructing capital ships and to use them as they wished; there was no need for the adoption of a special measure behind which, an ulterior motive might lie concealed. That was the position of the Liberal party, and it is a position of which every Liberal in this country has reason to be proud. Had this policy been carried out, there would have been a very different story when the war came on, as to the part played by Canada's naval service, in addition to the magnificent part which was played by her army.

Is that the Government's
policy of to-day also?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That was
the policy of the Liberal party in 1910; it was the policy of the Liberal party in 1912; it was the policy of the Liberal party in 1914, and it is the policy of the Liberal party to-day. It is the policy the Liberal party will continue to advocate as the one effective and only reasonable poliey for this country.

Do I understand the
Prime Minister aright? Is it the Government's proposal to construct these fleets immediately?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I drew my
hon. friend's attention to the purposes of the Naval Service Act and to the Liberal policy, which aims, let me repeat, at the creation of a naval department, the establishment of a naval reserve, the creation of a volunteer naval force, and the construction of ships to act in co-operation with the British navy at such times, as the Government of Canada may place them at the disposal of the Admiralty. That is a broad policy; it is a policy not for one day or one month or one year; it is a policy for the years that lie ahead. When it was promulgated it had regard to a situation which existed or was believed to exist at the time; it was put forward in the light of the financial condition of the country, in the light of world conditions at the time. And that policy will be carried on in the light of our country's present financial condition and in the light of conditions generally throughout the world. That is the policy which we believe it is most advisable to follow, alike in the interests of this country and in the interests of the Empire.
Does the naval expenditure as represented in the estimates presented this session represent Canada's proper proportion in the way of naval expenditure within the Empire?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I shall be
glad to take that point up later. The question of proportion must be considered in relation to all the other aspects of the subject. It is perfectly proper to consider it in relation to the naval and military expenditures that we are called upon to make at the present time, in relation to our public debt, to what we have still to meet in the way of obligations arising out of the war. We are entitled to take all these matters into consideration in undertaking to say what is wise and in the public interest at the present time, in the way of

further naval expenditure; and that is what we propose 'to do. But the broad policy is exactly as I have indicated it to my hon. friend. The Liberal party has had one policy, from the start, and that has been a permanent policy. It has never wavered in that policy; it has fought for it; it will continue to stand for it, and some day that policy will become the pride of this country as well as of the party that inaugurated it.
Now, Sir, that was the position in 1912. And after 1912, after this resolution with regard to the three dreadnaughts defeated, what did the Government do? They professed to believe in an emergency, but from that moment until the hour that war broke out, and until the war was over, nothing was done in any way to further the development of a naval service or-until the war had started-to put into commission the two ships which had been purchased by the Liberal Administration. As a matter of fact, if I recall the circumstances aright, when these ships were put into commission they played a very good part in the war- in a small way, it is true, but nevertheless a part of which we were all proud at the time.
So much for the period preceding the war and the intentions and purposes of the respective parties in the matter of naval policy. When the war was over, when the troops were being demobilized, when this country was being called upon to vote millions upon millions of dollars for the return of the men from overseas and to meet expenditure of further millions for pensions and the like, we naturally expected that at least a breathing time would be permitted, before we were asked to make further expenditures on naval account. I must say that for the first year after the war there was a slight cessation; the total expenditure on naval account in the year 1919-20 was $209,456, this amount being provided to keep up the services which the department was controlling and which related to branches of national administration other than those I have mentioned. In the following year, 1920-21, the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, under whom the Naval Department had been placed, came before Parliament, and in the main estimates, first of all, asked for an appropriation of $300,000. The press of the country announced that he had decided to demobilize the naval forces which then existed, and the country got the impression, that for a time at least, there was to be a little leeway in the matter of further 
Supply-Naval Service
expenditure on naval account. Then, much to the surprise of this House, within a very few days of the conclusion of the session, when Parliament had reasonable ground for the belief that its work was done, and most of the members were preparing to leave for their homes-on the 14th of June, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries brought dovyn a supplementary estimate of $2,200,000 for naval expenditure.
Here is what the minister said on March 25:
In vfew of Canada's heavy financial commitments and of the fact that Great Britain has not as yet decided on her permanent naval policy, and of the approaching Imperial conference, at which the question of naval defence of the Empire will come up for discussion between the home Government and the overseas dominions, it has been decided to defer in the meantime action in regard to the adoption of a permanent naval policy for Canada.
That sounded very logical and very reasonable. If it was sound logic and good reason on May 25, 1920, it is equally sound and equally good to-day, and it is a position, which this Government has taken with respect to naval expenditures-except, that the present Government has a permanent naval policy. The point to which we are # giving consideration at the moment is, in the light of present needs, in the light of existing world conditions, in the light of the fact that the Imperial Conference referred to has not been held, how far is the Government justified in going at the present time in making expenditures under the Naval Service Act?
We take the position that was taken by the Minister of Marine at that time, that there are heavy financial commitments of which this country and this Parliament have to take account, that Great Britain has not yet fully decided on her policy, and that an Imperial conference is to be held at which the question of naval defence will come up for discussion, between the home government and the overseas dominions. Hon. members opposite have always contended, that we should wait until there had been an Imperial conference before taking any steps that committed this Parliament very far in the matter of naval expenditure. I think they are right in that.
I think they are sound in their view that naval policy, so far as this country is concerned, should have, as one factor meriting consideration, the matter of possible cooperation with the other British dominions and with the United Kingdom in the event of any great and serious danger arising.
Supply-Naval Service

Possible co-operation, I say, but thus far, in regard to the question of existing naval armaments, there has been no Imperial conference held since the war.
But what did the minister say further; and now I come to the point that has a particular bearing on these very ships we have been discussing to-day:
The Government has decided to carry on a Canadian naval service along pre-var lines, and has accepted the offer of Great Britain of one light cruiser and two torpedo boat destroyers to take the place of the present obsolete and useless training ships, the Niobe and th$ Rainbow.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think this House was entitled a year or two ago, and I think it is entitled at the present time, to have some definite information with respect to these ships which were a so-called gift on the part of Great Britain. We have never been told why that gift was made to Canada, whether it was made at the instance of the British government, offering us ships which were never requested by us, or whether it was made at the instance of the government of the day making some suggestion to the government of Great Britain. Will my right hon. friend, who was Prime Minister and should know, tell the House the circumstances under which < these five ships were accepted from Great Britain?

I do not think I was
Prime Minister at the time the arrangement was made. I am not certain as to the date.
I know of no special arrangements at all except that Great Britain offered us the five ships, which were accepted. I remember there were negotiations as to the character of the ships, and finally these were agreed upon as being modern and useful for our purpose. I know of no other arrangement at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Does it not
strike my right hon. friend as a somewhat curious circumstance,-because even if he were not Prime Minister at the time, he was a member of the government which accepted these ships,-that he should not be informed about any agreements or arrangements with respect to the offer or its acceptance?

I do not know that there were any special arrangements. I do not know why there should be.
Mr.' MACKENZIE KING: Is it not an amazing thing, that the acceptance of a gift, which involved an expenditure of something like $2,500,000, should have been

The government of the day intended to maintain them and to use them for their purposes, or they would not have accepted them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Did the government of the day so inform the British government?

Not that I know of.
So far as I know, the British government did not exact anything. They had some confidence in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Then we come to this position. The government of the day intended to put five ships into commission, involving an annual expenditure of $2,500,000, but the government of the day had no authority from Parliament for that purpose, nor did it ever present to Parliament, as a matter for discussion, the question as to whether they were justified in taking that particular step.
Mr, MEIGHEN: The minister knows we could not put a ship in commission or spend a dollar until Parliament had voted it for the purpose. We came to Parliament to get the vote, and Parliament voted it.
After having accepted the ships.
Very well, but Parliament did not have to vote it. Parliament is not voting it to-day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What was
the position my right hon. friend and his colleagues took in Parliament? It was this: If you refuse to vote this money, you repudiate this gift on the part of the British government.
Will the hon. gentleman read that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I could if I had the time to look it up. It would not take long to find it. That was the nature of the argument that was presented at the time.
Now, the position is this: In regard to naval policy, more perhaps than in regard to any other policy of which this Parliament has reason to take account, we contend that what is to be done and what shall not be done shall be a matter of discussion in this House and in this Parliament. That is the essential condition. But such an op-

portunity was never given to the Canadian people or to their representatives in Parliament with respect to these ships, nor was it given to the Parliament of Great Britain with respect to the ships that were given away. It was all a matter of secret arrangement between some right hon. gentleman associated with my right hon. friend, and one or two members of the British administration. The position we took at that time, and the position we take to-day is that the acceptance of these five ships committed this country to a certain course for years to come. We contended that before that obligation was consummated, Parliament should have been fully informed and should have had an opportunity to express its views. To the extent to which we of the Liberal party had an opportunity to express our views, we protested against the acceptance of these ships. We asked that they should not be put into commission at that time because we regarded them under the circumstances as a very expensive and unnecessary luxury. May I quote to the House, a brief extract or two from the remarks which I ventured to make as leader of the Opposition at that time with reference to the acceptance of these ships? I quote from the Hansard of the 14th of June:
I shall not attempt at the moment any criticism with respect to the acceptance ot this gift beyond mentioning that on these matters Parliament should in the first instance be consulted. The people of Canada have a right-through their representatives in this Parliament-to say whether or not at tips time the country should be committed to an expenditure such as this afternoon the minister has announced we are to be asked to meet. We have this right as a Parliament and the country should not have been committed to this course by secret negotiations made by the Prime Minister and his colleagues during the course of the last year, or the last few months. All that we have been told this afternoon is that negotiations have been carried on by the Prime Minister and his colleagues and some members of the British Admiralty. With this comes the announcement that certain commitments have been made by Order in Council, in regard to none of which this Parliament has had the slightest intimation.
And further:
A wave of indignation will sweep over this Dominion when the statement goes forth that, now that the war is over, at a time when we are considering in what way we can retrench on naval and military expenditures, and after the professions they have made, the Government have announced a programme involving an expenditure such as that which has been mentioned to-day, and more especially when the country learns that this has been done without Parliament having had any voice in the matter one way or the other. That, Mr. Speaker, is the exception X wish to take at the moment to the programme of the minister and of the Government. 1 shall, at the moment, say nothing
as to whether it is right that Canada should or should not do this or that. I believe that Canada should assist in naval matters-in coast defence and co-operation in other ways-but I say that the country has a right to have its policy determined on the floor of Parliament and not in secret councils of the Cabinet. Certainly in this matter, the Government have shown a complete indifference to the rights of the people, through their representatives in this House, in giving no opportunity whatever for the country to say whether or not these ships shall be accepted, whether or not the expenditures, they will involve shall be incurred, whether or not we are to launch upon such a programme at the present time. All that the Government have said is that they have no policy, and will have no policy, until after the Imperial Conference in 1921.
What was said in that connection from one source was said also by a number of other speakers who addressed the House at that time. May I read just one paragraph from a speech made by my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance, in the course of the same debate? Here is what the Minister of Finance said at the time with reference to these particular ships:
I say that there are reasons why we should not proceed further in this matter. The first is that we have not the money; second, there is the fact that we are not in a position to-day to declare any extensive naval policy; and last, but not least, is the fact that if you accept these ships from Great Britain you accept a white elephant. We should say with great gratitude that we appreciate the offer which Great Britain has made us but that we cannot find it possible at the present time to avail ourselves of it. Later on we may have the ships when we can afford to undertake a definite policy in this direction. We are not going to ignore naval responsibility and refuse to take our share in naval affairs, but in view of all that has happened, let us have a breathing spell let us have time to think matters over, and let us devote the money to things more urgent than this.
That was the position the party took when in opposition; that is the position which we take to-day. We say, that there are more urgent matters; we say, there are demands for our money to-day greater than any that come within the circumference of this particular contribution for naval purposes.
But that is not all. Not only was this Parliament not consulted, not only was Canada placed under an obligation by the late government through forcing these expenditures on the country against its will, but when the British Parliament met, subsequent to these gifts being made to Canada, we find that the members of the British House took exception to the gifts being made without the Parliament of Great Britain having been consulted. That is the strange position into which the two coun-

What occurs to me is whether the committee is satisfied that important ships should be given even to our Dominions without the authority of Parliament. Has the Cabinet the power to
give away any of the ships of the British navy?
To this Mr. Stewart, the witness, replied:
I suppose there is no precedent.
Now that is the way in which these ships were obtained by Canada.

The Prime Minister will permit me this question: If I caught the reading carefully it referred to "gifts" what the Prime Minister is relating refers to "ships in their waters." That seems to be not applicable to the Canadian case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, my hon. friend can get what satisfaction he can out of that.
I am not seeking to get any satisfaction, I am trying to obtain information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will quote from the record again:
What happened was that the dominions made requests for certain vessels which were usually in their waters-
That does not say that in all cases the vessels were in their waters.
In our waters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think there is any distinction made as between vessels in Canadian waters and vessels in other waters.

It could not possibly refer to Canada. I do not know who made the proposals first, but I do know this, that the ships first under consideration were ships that were not of a modern character,

The minister himself says the ships are of a value that cannot be scrapped even now, and he is going to put them to use. Why then does the Prime Minister stand there and say they are of no use at all, that they are only of use for scrap?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not saying they are only of use for scrap. It is as far as the British government is concerned, that they are only of use for scrap. This is a statement that was made under oath before the Public Accounts Committee of the British House of Commons.
It cannot refer to our ships.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is as clear as it possibly can be to what ships it relates.
I may say, that in case of the larger item, gifts of ships to the dominions
It may not be Canada, it may mean ships that were in their waters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The statement does not say that it is ships that were in their waters. The statement speaks of "the dominions", and that embraces Canada. It does not speak of ships "in our waters" but "in their waters." It includes all the ships as definitely as any statement can.
When were these ships in our waters before?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Speaking of the gifts as a whole, the statement refers to ships that were usually in their waters. The witness evidently tried to find some excuse to save the face of the Cabinet; but what the Public Accounts Committee of the House of Commons did was to take exception to the gifts being made without parliament having been consulted. However, I think all hon. members will be able to judge of the value of the evidence for themselves. The evidence as taken before this committee is exactly what is implied in this statement. My hon. friend has no other statement to give us than that the ships were offered by the British government. Well, according to the statements I have quoted, even that was entirely without precedent. If the British government had kept the ships they would probably have been of use to them only as scrap; they had served their purpose and it suited the government's purpose to give them away. The point we
119J
are taking exception to is that the government of my hon. friend and his predecessors bring into this country ships which might have been consigned to the scrap heap by the British authorities, but upon the upkeep of which we must expend two and a half million dollars, if not more, and this without ever consulting Parliament as to whether or not the ships should be accepted.
I come next to the Imperial Conference of Premiers which my right hon. friend attended. Let me say that the position which the Government takes to-day is precisely in accord with that which is set out in the resolution of the Conference of Premiers that has been quoted by my right hon. friend. The resolution reads:
That while recognizing the necessity of cooperation among the various portions of the Empire to provide such naval defence as may prove to be essential for security, and while holding that equality with the naval strength of any other power is a minimum standard for that purpose, this conference is of opinion that the method and expense of such cooperation are matters for the final determination of the several parliaments concerned, and that any recommendations thereon should be deferred until after the coming Conference on Disarmament.
Let me say a word in regard to the first part of this resolution, which reads, "recognizing the necessity of co-operation among the various portions of the Empire." If that has any meaning other than reference to co-operation as the word is used in the Canadian Naval Service Act, I will not accept the further meaning. If it implies an obligation beyond that which, this Parliament itself has been ready to assume, in the matter of national defence, then, I contend it goes beyond rights or powers which the leader of the government of the day had any right to assume in giving assent to the resolution. I asked the right hon. member whether it did go further than this Parliament had recognized its obligation to go, and he answered me in the negative that it did not, and I accept his word for it. He has referred to a resolution of April 27 which was adopted, but I will quote it because it further states the Liberal position on the matter of naval service. It reads as follows:
That the House while recognizing the propriety of Canada being represented at any Imperial Conference or Conferences of the Prime Ministers of the Empire that may be called, desires to record its opinion, that at the coming conference no steps should be taken in any way involving any change in the relations of Canada to other parts of the Empire, and that in view of the present fin-

anclal position of Canada no action should be taken implying any obligation on the part of Canada to undertake new expenditures for naval or military purposes.
That was the Liberal position before my right hon. friend attended the Imperial Conference as a representative of Canada. I understand from his remarks that that resolution was unnecessary, that in no way did he exceed the intent or purport of it in representing this country at the Imperial Conference. The Government of to-day, propose to accept that interpretation of his action while at the conference, and not to recognize any obligation, which may directly or indirectly have been made as respects. Canada, implying military or naval expenditure beyond what had already been agreed to, before my right hon. friend attended the conference. I should like my right hon. friend to tell the House frankly and openly if he feels that is other than a just and proper interpretation, or whether he thinks additional obligations have been put on the Dominion by reason of his having been at the Conference of Prime Ministers.

As I have stated, the resolution could not be worded more clearly. It means precisely what it says. It places no obligation upon us at all. It clearly says that what we do, in point of character and in point of amount, is for us to say. Any obligation we are under is bounded only by our sense of duty and right and honour in the Empire.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is quite clear. I wish to draw attention of hon. members to one or two matters in conclusion. First of all, in regard to the ships accepted in the manner I have described, we have consistently taken the position, that this Parliament should have been consulted, before those ships were accepted, and I think it is only right and proper at the present time, that Parliament should understand that we recognize no obligation in virtue of any action taken by our predecessors, without having consulted Parliament or without having for it the approval of Parliament.

That would include
moral obligations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is a
matter which may be considered wholly apart from anything else, but I contend my hon. friend had no right-and I am assuming from his word that he is stating that he did not-to obligate this country
[Mr. Mackenzie King.l
in any particular, at the last Conference of Prime Ministers, beyond what had already been formerly agreed to in this House. This resolution states:
The conference is of the opinion that the method and expense are matters for final determination of the several parliaments concerned.
That is the position we are taking at the present moment, that while we have our naval policy, it is our duty to come to Parliament and discuss the expense which will be involved in bringing any part of it into practice or full play. More than that, we take also the position that the views expressed in the next recommendation or the next statement is a sound and proper one to have regard for: namely, that any recommendations thereon should be deferred until after the coming conference on disarmament. That is one of the strongest reasons why the government of the day, should not have accepted any ships which involved additional naval expenditure by this country. The conference of prime ministers thought it well to state that, before any of the dominions undertook to do anything of a material character with respect to their respective naval policies, they should have regard to the conference of disarmament and what actions might grow out of that conference. We have had regard for the Disarmament Conference and part of our policy is the result of what took place at that conference. The Minister of Naval Defence has this afternoon given a quotation from a document that I laid on the Table of the House on the 11th April. It is the memorandum of the British Government on Anglo-French relations; I wish to repeat one sentence to which he referred, because it gives the reason why the Government of to-day thinks it unwise this country should incur further expenditure in the matter of submarines. These submarines it should be recalled, were accepted by the Prime Minister of the day, without I think, his even consulting his cabinet, certainly without any consulting of Parliament. They were put into commission and we have been paying the cost of them ever since. What is stated in the British memorandum? It is-
The British opinion, however, based on four years' experience, is that submarines are
effective only against merchant ships and are ineffectual otherwise as instruments either of attack or defence.
We do not feel justified, in view of the opinion expressed to the world in that mem-

Supply-Naval Service
orandum, in having as part of our policy the maintenance of submarines. But if that is not sufficient, I would refer my right hon. friend and hon. members opposite to the report of Sir Robert Borden at the Conference on the Limitation of Armaments held at Washington. Let me read Sir Robert's own words in reference to the use of submarines, on page 22 of the report which has already been presented to Parliament and of which hon. members have copies. The report says:
An important proposal by the pritish Empire delegation, which enlisted universal attention, should be specially mentioned here. It looked to the complete abolition of the submarine. The pro-posal was formally placed on record in the following terms:
"The British Delegation desires formally to place on record its opinion that the use of submarines whilst of small value for defensive purposes, leads inevitably to acts which are inconsistent with the laws of war and the dictates of humanity, and the Delegation desires that united action should be taken by all nations to forbid their maintenance, construction, or employment".
It precipitated a remarkable discussion to which the widest publicity was given. To those who have acquired any intimate knowledge of the character of submarine warfare, the conclusion expressed in the proposal seems irresistible.
It was effectively argued that for defence the submarine is of relatively small value, while, on the other hand, the very nature of the craft and the physical necessities under which it operates are such that its use in war inevitably produces acts inconsistent with the plainest dictates of humanity.
I ask my hon. friends, in view of a statement such as that, in view of the Conference of the prime ministers having expressed the view that regard should be had, in any future naval policy, for the work of the Conference on the Limitation of Armaments at Washington, whether this Government would be justified in continuing to keep in commission the submarines accepted by the late government.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, let me say that the Government is quite as sensible as any of its predecessors of the obligation that rests upon this country as a nation and as part of the British Empire. It is fully cognizant of its obligation of service on land and sea, and its obligations, moral and otherwise, in every other respect. But we feel that every obligation can be rightly discharged only in the light of conditions as they exist, and the conditions to-day are entirely different throughout the world, and in our own country in particular, from those that prevailed prior to the war. To hear the argument advanced by my right hon.
friend (Mr. Meighen) one would imagine that the position was exactly the same it) the world to-day as it ever was. He dwelt at considerable length and eloquently on the position of Great Britain, who had scrapped so many ships; but he never said a word about the ships of other nations having been correspondingly reduced in numbers. He did not say anything about one great menace having been completely abolished.

My hon. friend
evidently did not hear me. I referred to the reduction of the United States navy and to the destruction of the German fleet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My right
hon. friend is quite right in saying that he referred to those matters; but he did not mention them in the connection I mean. I am speaking of his remarks as regards the necessity of Canada recognising its moral obligation towards Britain. In that connection he spoke at great length of how Great Britain had reduced her different fleets and of the consequent necessity lot Canada to give so much more to meet the situation than she would otherwise be obliged to do. Now, as hon. members are well aware, the condition of the world today is vastly different from what it was previous to the war, particularly in the matter of navies. The German navy has been completely destroyed. What menace is there at the present time that threatens any part of the British Empire on sea? Does my right hon. friend think that Canada, or Great Britain, or any other part of the British Empire is going to be attacked by the United States, by France, or by Japan? These countries have recently entered intoa solemn agreement together with Great Britain for the very purpose of helping to obviate the possibility of war arising between them. Is there any danger from Italy or from any of the smaller countries? Have we not a right, in considering expenditures here, to take all these facts into account? Have we to assume that at all times a situation will exist such as existed prior to 1912? I think the Government is justified in taking,-indeed, I think it would be seriously lacking in its sense of duty if it did not take-very much into account the changed conditions in the world to-day, and, in addition to that, the changed condition of our own treasury and the way in which these matters are likely to he viewed by the taxpayers of the country. We can build up the British Empire in no better way than by helping to make a
Supply-Naval Service

united, a contented and a happy people. And when my right hon. friend talks about moral obligation, let me remind him that the best defence is no offence, where you can avoid it, to other countries. I thought of that the other evening when the right hon. gentleman talked about exclusion with respect to a great Asiatic power. If he wants to build up the Empire and at the same time to avoid the necessity for military expenditures let him treat courteously the other great powers and there will be less need for munitions and instruments of war. Let us establish that good-will by which the building up of vast armaments is eliminated altogether, instead of creating the ill-will which, throughout the whole of history, has been responsible for wars among the nations of the world. We are sensible of our moral obligations and we shall do our utmost to meet them; and what I have just indicated is one of the most effective ways of doing so. There is the further position taken all along, that it would be the part of wisdom and prudence on the part of the Government to wait until after another Imperial Conference before beginning to launch out on any scheme in connection with naval matters, in the direction my hon. friends have indicated, which may not be acceptable and which may result, as the submarine business has done, in a waste of public money to no purpose. These are the reasons which have actuated the Government in seeking at the present time a retrenchment in the matter of naval and military expenditures. We are seeking to consolidate the great departments of defence and to bring into one department, under one minister, the naval, the military and the air forces. What is the object? Avowedly, it is for the purpose of economy; avowedly, for the purpose of retrenchment. If we are ever to have retrenchment in military and naval expenditures this is the one moment in which it is possible to bring about something of that character. The Government regards that as its first duty, its first obligation. It is sensible of all its larger duties and obligations, but it feels that it will best serve the interests of the British Empire as a whole when it helps to enlist, in the matter of defence, whether on land or sea, the sympathies of all our citizens throughout the Dominion, rather than antagonize their just sentiments by experiments of different kinds which will only tend to increase taxation and render no effective service in the long run.

I do not desire to make anything in the nature of a speech in reply to my hon. friend, but merely to refer to three or four matters which he has brought up, in order that what I said before may not, through any fault of mine, be misunderstood. The Prime Minister's address consisted in the main-at least half of it did-not jo much in a review of the history of this question as in a continuous and bitter attack upon his political opponents and upon the stand they have taken from time to time upon the question. I sought to make a review, but I place myself in the judgment of the committee if, in the course of that review, I made any attack whatever or any attempt to enlist the sympathies of the House on behalf of one or other of the old parties. I made no comparison of the relative merits of one course as against the other. I refrained from doing so, not because I did not think I was capable of doing it. Were the occasion appropriate, were there any object to be served, I think I might employ as forceful an argument- I venture to suggest, in all respect, a more effective argument, one more faithful to the facts-than did the Prime Minister. That was not my purpose.
Oh, oh.
The usual tactics are becoming apparent. How different is the course pursued on one side of the House from that followed on the other.
That is because you are up.
I think it is; I think that is the reason. Cannot hon. members meet me any other way than that?
It is your fault, not ours.

I sought to review the history of the question only that the perspective might appear and that the committee might the better judge what we should do now. That is all. I made no attack upon the principle of the Naval Service Act; nor, in the whole history of the debates in this House since I became a member of it, have I ever made an attack upon that principle. My position has been that under the act you could not develop a navy, either in point of ships or in point of men, in time to meet any situation that might confront us. I have made no attack on the principle of the act as being a sound one applicable to this country. In fact, I affirm that in 1918 at the conference Sir Robert Borden himself proposed, on behalf of the dominions, that the proper line to pursue by way of a per-

Supply-Naval Service
manent policy was even in the direction of the Naval Service Act. In so far as a Canadian naval service is embodied in the minister's proposal, I make no attack now. But policy consists not only in a statute, but in the actual proposals of the government as to what they are going to do under the statute. And it is in that respect that I make any attack. I propose to confine myself in what I say to that. I will not be drawn into the old discussions that took place years ago. We gain nothing by referring to them to-night. I want to discuss for a minute or two a few of the remarks of the Prime Minister as related to the point in issue.
On the lines of the Naval Service Act are these proposals adequate and worthy of our country? The Prime Minister attacks me very bitterly because I was a member of the Government that acceptd the free gift from the British Government of five ships, and he says that we never should have accepted them without coming to Parliament, because by that acceptance we obligated this country to maintain those ships.
The government of the day in accepting those ships certainly intended to maintain them and use them for the purpose for which we accepted them. But we could not do so until we came to Parliament and got authority. We could not pay a dollar of the cost in discharge of the obligation of this country without coming to Parliament and securing that authority. We came to Parliament, and we got authority for that purpose-just the same authority as the Government is seeking to-day.
Is it the argument of the hon. gentleman : But Parliament could not help itself. You by merely letting these ships into your ports obligated the country morally co maintain and operate these vessels. Is that the argument? I do not think it is. But if it is, how is his Government discharging the moral obligation now by abandoning the ships? Their own conduct now shows that by the mere acceptance of the ships they do not consider that a moral obligation was incurred at all. That is their position, rightly or wrongly. If the obligation exists, how can they abandon those ships now?
Will my right hon. friend allow me a question? Does he not believe that Canada, like other nations, should disarm after the Washington Conference?
The hon. gentleman must have been asleep; I was on another subject altogether.
I was quite awake.

Then why does he want me to leave the subject I am discussing? We came to Parliament for authority to spend every dollar. I am not concerned as to the position of the British government. The British government parted with property; we parted with nothing; that is the difference. What they should have done is for them and their Parliament to say. The hon. member tries to read into some evidence that was given there the inference that the vssels we took were worthless. Well, the vessels are there to be seen. Those vessels are modern.
No, they are not; they are obsolete.

They are not as
modern as when they were built,-nothing ever is. After the Government has had these two trawlers, three or four years they will not be modern either. On that principle you would never get anything. Those vessels were modern in construction, they were oil-burning vessels. They were as modern as any that the British government had; that is to say, of their size and for their purpose. They are not, of course, capital ships, but they are useful for training purposes. The fact is they were good vessels when we took them over, they are good to-day, and the Government admits it by saying they are going to put them to use.

They were not going to be
kept in commission in England.

Very well. The British government may have had sufficient vessels without them; I know nothing about that; but I do know that they are well constructed, modern vessels.
The next thing my hon. friend says is-
How can my right hon. friend argue that England expects us to keep these ships in commission when she has been scrapping other ships?

England is scrapping
her ships to-day,-she has scrapped twenty-three or twenty-four. But does that imply that we are under no obligation in the matter of naval defence?
She does not need more ships.
She does not need more ships, but she needs to maintain a defensive naval force, and it is in the maintenance of that defence that I make my plea.

These were surplus ships.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think my right hon. friend really understands the point I wish to make when I spoke of the right of Parliament to pass on these matters. And would he say for one minute that his government had any right to deal with this naval question which related to post war policy?
Undoubtedly I say so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Where did you get that right?
The government of the day had to carry on all matters of policy. The government of the day in any event did not make any change in naval policy, none whatever.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Was it understood by the people of Canada when the Unionist government was formed that after the war was over part of its duty was to inaugurate a naval policy for post war times?
The Unionist government did not inaugurate a naval policy at all.
For once he is right.
But I am afraid my hon. friend will be censured very soon by his leader.
Do not worry.
What is the complaint?
The complaint is that the Tory party had no naval policy.

The Prime Minister's complaint is that it had. We simply carried on a system of training for the naval service, believing that was the best by way of permanent policy, and we carried it on on a scale that we thought fair. Certainly it was not on too great a scale; if there was any complaint it was that it was on too small a scale. We carried it on on a scale that we thought fair until the aggregate commitments of the Empire would be known. These aggregate commitments became known at the Disarmament Conference.

Now I come to my last point. After the Disarmament Conference, when the utmost efforts of Britain were put forward and assisted by this country, by Australia, by New Zealand, and the other British commonwealths, and, let me add, by the United States-after those countries had exerted their efforts to the utmost, still the obligations of Great Britain remained at the point I have named, with the approval'of those countries. Now, is Canada to stand up and through its Prime Minister say : Those countries do not know world conditions. Britain does not know world conditions, and sihe has assumed naval obligations that she does not need to assume at all. Do the Government take that position? I do not think they will now say so. We know what burden Great Britain has assumed, reduced by that conference after every effort of those peace-loving nations had been brought to bear- we know that the residuum is about $400,000,000 a year. The Prime Minister says that our fair share of that huge burden is $1,500,000, to be spent on training boys two or three weeks in drill halls and on trawlers watching seals in the Behring sea.

After the Disarmament Conference, after all the facts that could be known were known and all that could be done was done, Britain's obligations rested upon a parity with those of the United States, only on a parity, at a certain amount per annum, the maintenance of a certain size of navy costing so much per annum. We cannot say it is too much.
, No Canadian will say that Britain can afford to become a second-rate power in a naval sense. We cannot say it is too much. Now hon. members admitting that this minimum has been arrived at in the effort to reduce armaments, the only question for us to decide is what share of that aggregate would fairly and rightly under all conditions be the proportion of this country? That is the question before us.
The hon. member asks: What are we arming against? As I stated in the debate on the militia estimates, that is a question that never can be answered, and it is a question that, if it could be answered, might not wisely be answered. I am not going to point my finger, I would not if I could, to any special nation and say: There is a potential enemy. That is not the habit
of any civilized country; that is not our habit; we do not do that. We say now we are in the position where we should only do our share in the common defence proportionate to what we have to defend, proportionate to our strength to defend, our fair and reasonable share under all the circumstances of the case. That is all we have to decide. There are many things to be taken into account, and if I were to stand and argue all the considerations, it would take some time. But I say one manifest thing: Outside of Great Britain, for Great Britain is not the only country in the Empire, we cannot stand squarely in front of our fellow-citizens of other dominions and say that we are bearing our fair share of the burden under the conditions of to-day.
The Prime Minister says we should pursue a pacific policy. I agree with him to the full. He intimates that it has been my plan to carry discourtesy to other countries and to stir up strife. When was I guilty of that? When were any words of mine ever of that character in this House of Commons? None that I can recall, none certainly were ever intentionally so. This country cannot pursue too pacific a policy to suit me, nor can this Empire pursue too pacific a policy to suit me. This Empire and this Dominion must, in words, and in every other way, pursue a most courteous policy towards Japan and every other country, but courtesy is not inconsistent with reasonable guarantees as to our control of our immigration and reasonable guarantees as to the composition of our people. It need not be inconsistent at all. If it were so, then I would say we would do better to suffer something rather than to pursue any course that had even the appearance of hostility towards a great friendly power. But after all this is done, there remains a necessary defence for great countries. We know the magnitude and the aggregate of that defence to-day, and in all selfrespect I say that we ought to do our share.
