speechtext: I have no desire to take an arbitrary stand on the matter at all, but I do think hon. members of the House are beginning to feel that we ought to get through the work of the session. We have had a couple of days now on this estimate, and I doubt very much if there are any other hon. members who wish to speak besides my hon. friend. If there are, and they will rise, and I see there is an appreciable number, I am quite agreeable to adjourning, but if it is only my hon. friend I think we should go on.

I think the Prime Minister is wholly unfair in putting me in that light, as if I was simply rising for the purpose of delaying this vote. That is not my intention at all. I consider this is one of the most important questions before Parliament. It is a matter that might very properly come before the House in the form of a resolution on going into Supply and be the occasion of a full dress debate in the House for days with profit. The leader of the Government has repeatedly enunciated as one of his fundamental principles that he musit consult Parliament and now he infers just because three or four members of the House have spoken, certainly not more than six, on this important matter, that it may be disposed of without further discussion.
I listened with a great deal of patience and attention to the discussion to-day and also to the very brief discussion,-not a whole day's discussion as my hon. friend the Prime Minister suggests-on a previous occasion. The minister introduced this item with a very brief speech and the leader of the Opposition stated that it was so important he would like time to consider it. Then we meet this afternoon and have a further discussion of it. I regret that the discussion this evening particularly in the address of the Prime Minister should have been taken up with a review, not so much of historic facts connected with the naval question, but a review rather of the controversial points. Now what I wish to suggest to the Government is this: That a rehash of old political discussions and debates in this House of the naval problem will get us to no very useful conclusion, but I do think that the time has arrived when we as a Parliament, and when Canada as a country, should face this problem, and should face it seriously, [DOT] and endeavour, as far as possible, to arrive at some conclusion commensurate with the importance of this Dominion and with the measure of her obligations.
Now I wish to draw attention to the question from this angle: First, I ask the question, is it Canada's desire to remain an integral part of the British Empire? To that I think there is only one answer which will be immediately given by every hon. member in this House, and I think by almost everyone within the confines of the country, and that answer is in the affirmative-that we do so desire, and that there is no wish to weaken the ties of Empire. Very well, let us accept that. Then we take the next step, which seems to me to be a logical

one and ask: Are we then as a member of the Empire, as a member of this commonwealth of nations called the British Empire, to assume that portion of the obligations of defence of empire which properly rests upon us? That seems to me to be the next point. If we admit that we are, and I have not heard a word to the contrary, then, by a logical sequence, we come to the next point: Is the estimate before us to be considered as a reasonable discharge of that responsibility? Now let us examine that briefly for a minute.
My hon. friend the Prime Minister, not only to-day but repeatedly, has laboured the point of our moral obligation. He has also queried the right hon. leader of the Opposition on this point: Did he obligate Canada to any specific obligation or responsibility in the recent conference at London? That seems to me to be begging the question. The point that the Prime Minister and his Government should determine is this: Are we obligated at all, is there any moral obligation resting upon us? If there is a moral obligation resting upon us, does not that imply a corresponding practical or political obligation that we should discharge or else be derelict in our duty? It is not a question as to whether the leader of the Opposition when he was prime minister, made for us any specific commitment in London. That is not the question. The question before this House, and the question the people of the country are seeking leadership on, is: What is the measure of the obligation of Canada at this time?
Now, I wish to take another step to a point which has already, I think, been effectively brought forward by the leader of the Opposition but of which I will at least take the liberty of repeating. It is this: The British Empire, represented by the Imperial government, in the recent Washington Conference came to a point in naval disarmament beyond which it said it could not go

which the naval armament could be reduced, which is admitted to be the minimum.

Well, my hon. friend
speaks of the responsibility of Great Britain. I want to know what he means by Great Britain in this connection? Or what responsibility Canada has towards Great Britain?

I made a statement to this effect: That at the Washington Conference a point was reached where it was agreed, not only on the authority of the British Empire but also on the authority of other members of the conference, that disarmament could not safely go below a certain point. That point represents a burden on the taxpayers of Great Britain of some $400,000,000 annually. Now then, it seems to me we have reached a basis of argument on this point where we come to a practical question. The question, as I have stated, is this: Are we obligated; are there any obligations resting on Canada in this connection? The Prime Minister has admitted that there are obligations; he has admitted that we must take our place as a member of the Commonwealth of the British Empire in this question of naval armament. In the face of the fact that Britain is maintaining naval defence for the Empire at the expense of $400,000,000 a year the question arises-is a million and a half an adequate amount for Canada to contribute towards that expense? I contend that it is not only inadequate but that it is not conmmensu-rate with the dignity of the country.
Now let me turn for a moment to some arguments advanced by gentlemen opposite. The minister in the first place scrapped the whole of the new Canadian navy-that is the five ships presented to Canada by the Mother Country, and put into operation and commission by the previous government. Then he pointed out that this unit was useless so far as naval work was concerned. He, however, modified that today by admitting that the unit might be

useful for training purposes, that it might be useful for representing Canada in some parts of the world where her interests needed attention and protection; and furthermore he admitted that Canada's interests and obligations demanded the existence of this unit, or portions of it. What sense then is there in Canada abandoning this somewhat limited and small unit in the face of the admission that we have work for it to do, in the face of the obligation undoubtedly resting upon us? In the face of the recognition by the minister's action to-day that there is a need for some naval unit in Canada, what is the sense of abandoning the unit we have? Some hon. gentlemen to-day asked to what extent should we go? It is not for the members of the Opposition to state to what extent we should go; but I think we can, as a parliament, take this position: Until a further Imperial Conference is held we should maintain the unit that we already have in commission. That, I think, is a safe and reasonable position to take.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) to-day made quite an argument on the general basis of disarmament. He pointed out that the world was disarming, and therefore Canada should disarm. That we should present to the world a peace loving people, that we should not for one moment pretend that we are in sympathy with or in harmony with the maintenance of national defence at all. I think the House might very properly- and this has not been referred to by any previous speakeT-turn its attention to the conditions and political activities in Europe to-day. Turn for a moment to the situation at Genoa, which it had been hoped, would usher in a new era, which my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) referred to, out of which it was hoped some solution might be reached of the economic problems of Europe, but, as a matter of fact, it is admitted to-day, by all the nations participating in that conference, that very little more than a complete failure has resulted from that meeting, but that is not all. If we turn to Germany and Russia, we find a new international treaty entered into by two of the greatest nations of the world, one of which has to-day under arms a force that, I think, is greater than the armed force of Germany before the war. She has an army running into millions, in active service, strung along her western frontier. The hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has properly stated that perhaps it is not a wise thing for members

in the House of Commons to refer to an apparently belligerent action or attitude on the part of any nation, but I think we are very unwise if we refuse to take cognizance of the existence of that tremendous armed force in Russia to-day. Then couple with that the fact that Germany has refused apparently, and is constantly refusing, to meet her obligations under the Versailles Treaty, that she is seeking to avoid those obligations, and add to that this fact that France-who is more intimately associated with the possible effect of such an alliance as I have referred to than any other nation,-expresses general alarm at these conditions; when you couple these three facts together, I think we have every right to say that there is an exceedingly disturbed state of mind in certain quarters of the world, which may be reflected at any moment in the form of active warfare. In the face of these facts, of our obligations as a part of the British Empire, of the admission of the Prime Minister that these obligations exist, it seems to me we are doing a most unwise thing, in not only cutting down, as we have done from last year, by a million dollars, but in scrapping the naval unit we have had, and in refusing to maintain that unit, and taking a decidedly backward step in connection with the matter of defence in Canada.

It has been regarded merely as an appendage of the railway system, with the result that Canada is today very many miles behind the times so far as her merchant marine is concerned. It has never had a chance, and if the Government would only have Lord Beatty, Admiral of the fleet, report on the question of the merchant marine and Canada's Naval Defence and see what could be done to nurse this important industry, I say that it would be a [DOT] splendid thing for the country, not only in the matter of freight rates but in the development of business generally.
I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. My hon. friend is talking about the merchant marine and we are discussing the naval estimates. I submit that he is entirely out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I rule that the point of order is well taken.
I submit that the hon. member was discussing the merchant marine to show that by its abolition, we should have a lot more money for naval expenditure, which means that the public-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. member that the ruling of the Chair has been given, and while it would have been competent for him before to discuss the point of order raised, he is out of order now.

I am urging the Government to bring down their naval policy. It is humiliating to have this two-penny halfpenny policy for a people of nine or ten millions, especially in view of the record the Canadian people made in this war. It simply means that we are sponging on the British people for naval and land defence. I would advocate a broad-minded policy, and it would really be an economy, if we had a proper shipbuilding programme for the lakes. It would help to solve not only the merchant marine problem, but the transportation problem, and unemployment, and would give us naval defence, and our ships would be able to sail the seven seas and

Supply-Naval Service
get some of the trade which this country should get as a result of the war. Certainly we are not getting the proportion now that we should get. I wish to quote from a little book called "The Fleets behind the Fleet" by W. Macneile Dixon, Professor in the University of Glasgow, to show that the great industrial expansion of Great Britain has not been due to free trade and Cob-denism but has been contributed to largely by the union of coal and steel and by the merchant marine. I say that every dollar spent on the merchant marine is a dollar spent on naval defence and for the expansion of trade and commerce, and that is also the view of this writer. He says that Canada should take a leaf out of the book of the Mother Country in this respect and goes on to speak of the merchant marine and the Royal navy.
The Royal navy is the heir of the merchant service, the inheritor of its fighting spirit and tradition. Not till Victoria's reign was any clear line of division drawn between the merchant sailor and the man-of-war's-man.
Histories as they have too often been written, obscure the vision and provide a false perspective. Faithful chronicles no doubt of the red-letter days of battle, but how few and far between were the battles in our long naval wars! Too often the histories speak of the navy as if it were a thing apart, a mere fighting instrument, and forget to tell us of the fleets behind the fleet: of the merchant sailors and the fishermen, the pioneers and the builders of our sea-supported confederacy.
These "traders", it was said of the Elizabethan seamen, "escaped the notice of kings and chroniclers.' Nevertherless, it was those men who saved England and America from becoming provinces of Spain.
The "navy" as we call it, what has history to say of it? That until the reign of Henry VIII, the pious founder of the Koyal navy, it was, in fact, neither more nor less than England's mercantile marine. As for Elizabeth's tall ships and proud captains, Drake and Hawkins and Frobisher and many another, they were stout merchant skippers, and of the fleet which met the Great Armada, near upon two hundred sail, but thirty-four belonged to the Queen's navy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend intends to speak very much longer, 'perhaps he would let me know, and then I can say what I have to say.
I would say to the Prime Minister I shall be glad to talk for one, two or three days, if necessary and advisable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The reason I asked my hon. friend the question was because I think there has been some misunderstanding as to the nature of a remark I made at the time the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) got up to speak. I intimated then that that I was
quite prepared to stay here all night to get through the debate in order to get on with the business of the House. I understand that hon. gentlemen opposite have construed that as a threat on the Government's part to keep this committee sitting all night if need be, and that some of them have arranged to have a series of speeches running well on to the morning. Now I have no desire whatever to have any remark of mine construed as a threat-nothing could be further from my mind than such an intention. I did say, and I repeated it later on, that I thought most of the members of the House were anxious to get through with business and we would do so by bringing to a close, if possible, to-night a debate which has been going on for a couple of days. I certainly feel that the House has got an entirely wrong impression of what I had in mind if it thought my words implied a threat in any way. The statement I made was that if there were a desire to continue, and if members on the other side would so indicate by rising I would be quite willing the debate should be adjourned. Only the hon. njember for Centre Vancouver rose. I desire that there shall not be any misunderstanding as to the attitude of the Government. We have every desire to give every hon. member who wishes to speak the opportunity to place his views before the House. If, therefore, there are several hon. members who still wish to speak I am quite willing that my hon. friend who now has the floor should adjourn the debate, and that the committee should rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Then I move that the committee rise and report progress.

I did intend to say a few words, but I wish to say that I am not in any combine to detain the House. Unless I had something that I thought would be of practical use in the debate I would take no part in it, I do not think that any hon. member can say that I unnecessarily detain the House.
I would also like to explain that there is no understanding of the kind alluded to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It has been moved by Mr. Church that the committe rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I am
Supply-Naval Service

generally very easy to get along with but I do not think the Opposition is treating me in a matter that is exactly fair. This is the third time Naval Estimates have been postponed. I postponed bringing them in at the request of the Opposition because [DOT]certain members were away. I did so because I wanted to accommodate them. The other day when these naval estimates were up, at the request of the leader of the Opposition I kept back this large item and set a day for its discussion, with the inference of course that the discussion would be concluded to-night. Now I find my convenience is not considered by the Opposition. I do not wish to complain but I have to go away to-morrow in order to fulfil an engagement. That means that my estimates will have to be further postponed, and I do not know for how long. If the courtesy is only going to be on one side I shall not be so courteous the next time.
I do not really understand the minister in making this reference.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do.

It is true that the
Oppositition asked for the postponement of the Defence Bill for a certain reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My estimates have been postponed three times at the request of the Opposition.

Postponements are
quite usual and are always granted. On Friday after the minister had stated his naval policy I suggested that we might go on with the other estimates, but I said I did not think this item should pass-that it was one of the most important matters; indeed by far the most important-that has been before this House. The minister should not have expected that the criticism should come immediately after his pronouncement of policy. The request for postponement was a most reasonable one.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Certainly.
What is the Opposition doing to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Talking against time
absolutely, as the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) certainly has been doing.

I do not think my hon. friend is fair in saying that. There has been no such purpose in view. The comment he makes is unfair and unworthy of him; there was no purpose whatever to obstruct the minister's estimates. There was a purpose to have an opportunity for

discussion on the part of those who wished to fairly discuss the estimates. That is the only stand we take. Furthermore, if the minister had been in the last Parliament he would know something about what obstruction and unfairness to the government was.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Allow me just a moment. I do not wish to be misunderstood, or to allow my right hon. friend to say that the postponment was in reference to some bill. On three distinct occasions I was asked to postpone the estimates and I did so.
I do not dispute that.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Well, I think there ought to be some little reciprocity.

If the minister wants the postponement we are quite willing to meet his wishes. If he is not able to be present to-morrow we are quite ready to take this matter up again on Thursday. We do not desire to unnecessarily exhaust any time at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I leave it to the judgment of the House whether my statement is correct or not.

I call the attention of the member for Hants to the fact that there is nothing before the committee at the prelsent time. The motion to report progress has been carried.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at one a.m., Wednesday.
